examiner_lens: AIBE tests recognition, not long analysis. Typical question styles: (1) 'Which section deals with...?'; (2) 'Which case laid down...?'; (3) numbers and periods (days, months, years, percentages); (4) 'Which of the following is correct/incorrect?'; (5) pair-comparison questions (void vs voidable, mortgage vs charge, lease vs licence, indemnity vs guarantee).

Because the paper is open-book, questions reward knowing WHERE to look quickly. Tab and underline: Contract Act Secs 2, 10, 15-19, 23-30, 56, 73-74; SRA Secs 6, 10, 14, 16, 20, 34, 38-42; TPA Secs 41, 43, 52, 53A, 54, 58, 59, 105-107, 111, 122-123; NI Act Secs 138-148; RFCTLARR Secs 24-26, 30, 101.
Examiners pick provisions that were amended recently (SRA 2018; NI Act 2015 and 2018), that are overlaid by landmark cases, and that carry crisp numbers.

modules.title: Law of Contract (Indian Contract Act 1872, with Sale of Goods and Partnership as bonus)

sections.title: Nature of Contract, Offer and Acceptance (Sections 1-10)
sections.summary: The foundation of the whole Contract Act. Expect 1-2 questions on definitions (Sec 2), essentials of a valid contract (Sec 10), communication/revocation of offer and acceptance (Secs 3-9), and the classic cases.
key_points: Sec 2(a) Proposal (offer): a person signifies to another his willingness to do or abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other. Sec 2(b) Promise: a proposal when accepted. Sec 2(c): the person making the proposal is the promisor, the person accepting is the promisee.

Sec 2(e) Agreement = every promise and every set of promises forming the consideration for each other. Sec 2(h) Contract = an agreement enforceable by law. So: Contract = Agreement + Enforceability. All contracts are agreements; not all agreements are contracts.

Sec 2(g) Void agreement = not enforceable by law. Sec 2(i) Voidable contract = enforceable at the option of one or more parties but not of the other(s). Sec 2(j) Void contract = a contract which ceases to be enforceable by law (becomes void). Note the sequence: void agreement is void from the start; a void contract was valid initially.

Sec 10 essentials: (1) free consent of parties, (2) competent to contract, (3) lawful consideration, (4) lawful object, (5) not expressly declared void. Writing/registration/witnesses where the law so requires.
Types by formation: express vs implied; executed vs executory; unilateral vs bilateral; e-contracts (valid under Sec 10A, Information Technology Act 2000).

Offer vs invitation to treat: display of goods in shop window, price lists, auction catalogue, advertisements to sell, and tender invitations are invitations to offer, not offers. A bid at an auction is the offer; fall of the hammer is acceptance (Sale of Goods Act Sec 64 / common law).
General offer: can be accepted by anyone who performs the conditions (Carlill). Notice of acceptance is not required where performance is the mode of acceptance.

Communication (Sec 4): communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Communication of acceptance is complete (i) as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him so as to be out of the power of the acceptor to withdraw it; (ii) as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. This is the POSTAL RULE of Indian law.

Communication of revocation is complete (i) as against the person who makes it, when put in a course of transmission to the person to whom it is made so as to be out of the power of the maker; (ii) as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge.

Sec 5: a proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards. An acceptance may be revoked at any time before communication of acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.

Sec 6, modes of revocation of a proposal: (1) by communication of notice of revocation by the proposer; (2) by lapse of the time prescribed (or a reasonable time if none); (3) by failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; (4) by death or insanity of the proposer, if the fact comes to the acceptor's knowledge before acceptance. Rejection by the offeree and a counter-offer also terminate the offer.
Sec 7: acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, and expressed in some usual and reasonable manner (unless the proposal prescribes the manner). A conditional acceptance is a counter-proposal.

Sec 8: performance of the conditions of a proposal, or acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise offered with the proposal, is acceptance. Silence is not acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley); a proposer cannot impose silence as acceptance.
Sec 9: promise is express if made in words; implied if made otherwise (conduct).

Communication of offer is necessary: ignorance of an offer means no acceptance. Lalman Shukla v Gauri Dutt: a person who finds a lost boy without knowing of the reward cannot claim it. (Contrast the English position in Williams v Carwardine.)
Social and domestic agreements between spouses/family members are presumed not to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour); commercial agreements are presumed to.

sections.title: Consideration and Privity (Sections 2(d), 25)
sections.summary: Indian law of consideration is wider than English law. Examiners love Sec 2(d), Sec 25 and the exceptions to 'no consideration, no contract'.
key_points: Sec 2(d): when at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains, or promises to do or abstain, such act or abstinence is called consideration. Key: 'at the desire of the promisor' AND 'promisee or any other person'.
Therefore in India consideration may move from a stranger (Chinnaya v Ramayya), but a stranger to the CONTRACT cannot sue (privity). English law requires consideration to move from the promisee.
Consideration may be past, present or future. Past consideration is valid in India (Sec 2(d) 'has done or abstained'), if done at the desire of the promisor.

Rules: must be real (not illusory), lawful, need not be adequate (Explanation 2 to Sec 25) but must be something of value; must not be physically impossible; must not be a pre-existing public duty (Collins v Godefroy); performance of existing contractual duty is generally not consideration (Indian law is more flexible).

Sec 25: an agreement made without consideration is void, unless: (1) it is expressed in writing AND registered under the law for registration of documents, and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other; (2) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do (past voluntary service); (3) it is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged (or his authorised agent), to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law of limitation.

Other exceptions to 'no consideration no contract': Sec 185 (no consideration needed to create an agency), Sec 63 (promise to remit performance/ accord), Sec 126-127 (past consideration for guarantee), completed gift (Sec 25 Explanation 1), bailment (gratuitous), charitable subscriptions acted upon (Kedar Nath v Gorie Mohamed).

Privity of contract: only parties can sue/be sued (Tweddle v Atkinson; Dunlop v Selfridge). Exceptions in India: (a) beneficiary under a trust/charge; (b) marriage settlements/family arrangements (Khwaja Muhammad Khan v Husaini Begum); (c) assignment of contract; (d) acknowledgment/estoppel; (e) agency; (f) covenants running with land; (g) contracts through statutory duty. M.C. Chacko v State Bank of Travancore (1969): a person for whose benefit a contract is made may sue to enforce it.

Doctrine of promissory estoppel: Central London Property Trust v High Trees; in India, Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v State of UP (1979): applies against the Government; need not show detriment, only alteration of position; cannot be used to compel the Government to act contrary to law and public interest.

'Consideration need not be adequate but must be real'. A question may ask which of these is 'not' valid consideration: past consideration is valid in India, but past voluntary act not at promisor's desire is not.

sections.title: Capacity to Contract and Free Consent (Sections 11-22)
sections.summary: Almost every AIBE paper has at least one question here: minor's agreements, coercion vs undue influence, fraud vs misrepresentation, mistake.
key_points: Sec 11: competent = (a) major (18 years under Indian Majority Act 1875; 21 years if a guardian of person/property has been appointed by court or the minor is under Court of Wards), (b) of sound mind, (c) not disqualified by any law (alien enemy, insolvent, convicts, foreign sovereigns/ ambassadors - subject to law).

Minor's agreement is VOID AB INITIO (Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose, Privy Council 1903). Consequences: no specific enforcement against the minor; no ratification on attaining majority (as a void agreement cannot be ratified by fresh consideration-less promise); minor cannot be estopped from pleading minority; no restitution under Sec 64/65 of money advanced (Sec 65 not applicable to minors per Mohori Bibee; but restitution possible if minor obtained property by fraud and property is identifiable - Equity doctrine, Khan Gul v Lakha Singh).

But: a minor can be a promisee/beneficiary, can be an agent (principal bound, agent not personally liable), can be admitted to benefits of a partnership (Sec 30 Partnership Act), and a minor's estate is liable for 'necessaries' supplied (Sec 68). Contracts by a guardian on behalf of minor, for minor's benefit and within guardian's authority, are enforceable (Mir Sarwarjan v Fakhruddin).

Sec 12: sound mind = capable of understanding the contract and forming a rational judgment as to its effect on his interests at the time of contracting. A lunatic may contract during lucid intervals; a sane man cannot contract when delirious or drunk.

Sec 13: consent = two or more persons agree upon the same thing in the same sense (consensus ad idem). Sec 14: consent is free when not caused by coercion (Sec 15), undue influence (Sec 16), fraud (Sec 17), misrepresentation (Sec 18) or mistake (Secs 20-22).

Sec 15 COERCION: committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (now read as the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023), or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement. It is immaterial whether the IPC/BNS is in force at the place where coercion is employed. Effect: contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Sec 19). Coercion may be by a stranger and may be directed at anyone. A threat to commit suicide is coercion (Ammiraju v Seshamma).

Sec 16 UNDUE INFLUENCE: contract induced by a relationship where one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses it to obtain unfair advantage. Presumed where: real/apparent authority (e.g., parent-child, guru-disciple, doctor-patient, solicitor-client, trustee-beneficiary), fiduciary relation, or the party is mentally distressed (illness, age). Sec 16(3): where the transaction appears unconscionable and the dominant party is in a position to dominate, the burden of proving no undue influence lies on the dominant party. Pardanashin women: special protection - the party must show the contract was explained and she understood.

Sec 17 FRAUD: act committed by a party (or with his connivance or by his agent) with intent to deceive another or to induce him to enter the contract: (1) suggestion as a fact of that which is not true by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (4) any other act fitted to deceive; (5) any act or omission the law specially declares fraudulent. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak (e.g., contracts uberrimae fidei such as insurance, or fiduciary relations) or the silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech. Derry v Peek: fraud means a false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly.

Sec 18 MISREPRESENTATION: (1) positive assertion not warranted by the information of the person making it, though he believes it to be true; (2) breach of duty which, without intent to deceive, gains an advantage by misleading another; (3) causing, however innocently, a party to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing.

Sec 19: contract caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Exception: if the consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence fraudulent under Sec 17, the contract is not voidable if the party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. This exception does NOT apply to fraud by active statement (Sec 19 Explanation). Sec 19A: undue influence - the contract may be set aside absolutely or, if the party has received any benefit, upon such terms as the court deems just.

Sec 20: where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact ESSENTIAL to the agreement, the agreement is void (bilateral mistake of fact). Illustration: Raffles v Wichelhaus (two ships named Peerless). Sec 21: mistake as to a law NOT in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact; a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India. Sec 22: a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties being under a mistake as to a matter of fact (unilateral mistake). Exceptions in case law: mistake as to the identity of the party/ nature of the document (non est factum).
Effect summary: coercion/undue influence/fraud/misrepresentation = VOIDABLE; bilateral mistake of essential fact = VOID; unilateral mistake = valid.

sections.title: Lawful Object, Void Agreements and Restraints (Sections 23-30)
sections.summary: Sec 23, 26, 27, 28 and 30 appear repeatedly, often with the exceptions and cases.
key_points: Sec 23: consideration or object is lawful unless: (1) forbidden by law; (2) of such a nature that if permitted it would defeat the provisions of any law; (3) fraudulent; (4) involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; (5) the Court regards it as immoral; (6) opposed to public policy. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

Public policy heads: trading with enemy, stifling prosecution, champerty/maintenance (in India, champerty is not per se void if bona fide - Ram Coomar Coondoo v Chunder Canto Mookerjee), marriage brokerage, sale of public offices, interference with administration of justice, agreements tending to create monopoly, unconscionable terms in standard form contracts (Central Inland Water Transport Corp v Brojo Nath Ganguly 1986).

Sec 24: if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void (subject to severability - if lawful part can be separated, it is enforceable).
Sec 25: see 1.2. Sec 26: agreement in restraint of marriage of any person other than a minor is void.

Sec 27: agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is, to that extent, void. Single statutory exception: sale of goodwill (a seller may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business within specified local limits, so long as the buyer carries on like business, provided the limits appear to the Court reasonable). Also Sec 54 Partnership Act (partners).

Indian law has no 'doctrine of reasonable restraint' for trade: any restraint is void, but restraint DURING the term of employment is valid (Niranjan Shankar Golikari v Century Spinning, 1967), and negative covenants operative during subsistence of contract can be enforced by injunction. Post-employment restraints are void (Superintendence Co of India v Krishan Murgai, 1981). Restraints on distributors/ exclusive dealing during contract are generally valid (Gujarat Bottling Co v Coca-Cola, 1995).

Sec 28 (as substituted in 1997): agreements void if they (a) restrict absolutely a party from enforcing his rights under or in respect of a contract by usual legal proceedings in ordinary tribunals, or limit the time within which he may enforce his rights; (b) extinguish the rights of a party or discharge any party from liability under the contract on the expiry of a specified period so as to restrict any party from enforcing his rights. Exceptions: agreements to refer future disputes to arbitration, and agreements to refer questions already arisen to arbitration. Exclusive jurisdiction clauses are valid if the chosen forum has jurisdiction and is not ousting all courts (ABC Laminart v A.P. Agencies, 1989; Hakam Singh v Gammon (India) Ltd, 1971).

Sec 29: agreements whose meaning is not certain or capable of being made certain are void. Sec 30: agreements by way of wager are void; no suit for recovering anything alleged to be won on a wager. Exception: horse-race prizes of Rs 500 or more (subscription/ contribution to a plate or prize). Collateral transactions to wagers are enforceable in most States (not in Maharashtra, where Bombay Act makes them void). Insurance and lottery are not wagers in the legal sense; Gherulal Parakh v Mahadeodas Maiya (1959): speculative contracts of forward sale/purchase are not wagers unless there is a common intention not to deliver goods and only pay differences.
Sec 56 (first paragraph): an agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void.
Immoral agreements: e.g., concubinage contracts, prostitution (Gherulal v Mahadeodas). Agreements to stifle prosecution (Sec 23): void if the offence is non-compoundable.

sections.title: Contingent Contracts, Performance, Time and Impossibility (Secs 31-58)
sections.summary: Doctrine of frustration (Sec 56), time as essence (Sec 55), tender (Sec 38) and contingent contracts (Secs 31-36) are the usual favourites.
key_points: Sec 31: contingent contract = a contract to do or not to do something if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen (insurance, guarantee, indemnity). Sec 32: contingent on an event happening cannot be enforced until the event has happened; if it becomes impossible, void. Sec 33: contingent on event NOT happening: enforceable when happening becomes impossible. Sec 34: event is the future conduct of a living person - deemed impossible when he does anything which makes it impossible within a definite time. Sec 35: contracts contingent on specified event happening within a fixed time become void if the event does not happen in that time (or becomes impossible). Sec 36: contingent agreements to do or not to do anything if an impossible event happens are void.

Sec 37: parties must perform or offer to perform their promises, unless performance is dispensed with or excused under this Act or any other law. Promisors' representatives are bound unless a contrary intention appears.

Sec 38: TENDER (offer of performance) - must be unconditional; at proper time and place; allow the promisee a reasonable opportunity to ascertain that the thing offered is the thing promised. Valid tender of performance, if refused, relieves the promisor of liability for non-performance and does not forfeit his rights. Tender of money must be of the exact amount (not obligatory to be accepted otherwise), and tender of money does not discharge the debt (the debt continues) but protects from costs/interest.

Sec 39: when a party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract unless he has signified his acquiescence in its continuance (anticipatory breach: Hochster v De la Tour; Frost v Knight).

Sec 40: contracts involving personal skill - the promisor must perform personally; Sec 41: acceptance of performance by a third person discharges the promisor even though the promisee is not bound to accept; Sec 42-45: devolution of joint liabilities and rights.

Secs 46-50: time and place: where no time is specified, performance within a reasonable time; where the promise is to be performed on a certain day without application by the promisee, the promisor may perform at any time during usual business hours on that day and at the place where the promise ought to be performed.

Sec 51-54: reciprocal promises. Sec 51: promisor not bound to perform unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform his reciprocal promise; Sec 52: order of performance; Sec 53: prevention by one party makes the contract voidable at the option of the other, who is entitled to compensation; Sec 54: when one party cannot perform the first part, the other need not perform.

Sec 55: TIME AS ESSENCE. If time is of the essence and a party fails to perform by the fixed time, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the promisee. If time is not of the essence, the contract is not voidable, but the promisee is entitled to compensation for loss caused by the delay. In sale of immovable property, time is NOT presumed to be of the essence (Chand Rani v Kamal Rani, 1993), though in rising markets courts take a strict view (K.S. Vidyanadam v Vairavan, 1997; Saradamani Kandappan v S. Rajalakshmi, 2011). Acceptance of late performance without notice of intention to claim compensation forfeits the right to compensation (Sec 55 last para).

Sec 56 FRUSTRATION: (1) an agreement to do an impossible act is void; (2) a contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful; (3) where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or with reasonable diligence might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must compensate the promisee for loss sustained through non-performance.

Indian courts apply Sec 56 as a positive law (not on implied-term theory): Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur (1954). Frustration is not available merely because performance becomes more onerous or expensive (Energy Watchdog v CERC 2017; Alopi Parshad v Union of India 1960). Doctrine applies to leases only in exceptional cases; it cannot apply where the contract contains a force majeure clause (the clause governs - Sec 32 route). Examples: Taylor v Caldwell (music hall burnt); Krell v Henry (coronation procession cancelled - frustration of purpose); Herne Bay Steam Boat v Hutton (distinguished).

Sec 57-58: reciprocal promises in alternative; Secs 59-61: appropriation of payments - the debtor's intimation prevails (Sec 59), failing which the creditor's right of appropriation (Sec 60), failing which payments are applied in discharge of debts in order of time (Sec 61).

landmark_cases.case: Satyabrata Ghose v Mugneeram Bangur (1954)
landmark_cases.principle: Sec 56 is exhaustive of frustration in India; 'impossible' includes practical impossibility; no implied-term theory.

landmark_cases.case: Taylor v Caldwell (1863)
landmark_cases.principle: Destruction of subject-matter frustrates the contract.

landmark_cases.case: Krell v Henry (1903)
landmark_cases.principle: Frustration of purpose.

landmark_cases.case: Energy Watchdog v CERC (2017)
landmark_cases.principle: Rise in coal prices does not frustrate a contract; commercial hardship is no excuse.

landmark_cases.case: Hochster v De la Tour (1853)
landmark_cases.principle: Anticipatory breach.

landmark_cases.case: Chand Rani v Kamal Rani (1993)
landmark_cases.principle: Time not of essence for immovable property sale unless expressly stated or implied.

common_traps: Sec 56 paragraph 2: contract becomes void on impossibility; the loss lies where it falls, but restitution is allowed under Sec 65.
Mere increase in cost or difficulty is NOT impossibility.
Time of essence for immovable property: not presumed; in commercial/mercantile contracts: presumed.
Sec 38 tender: tender of goods vs tender of money (money tender does not discharge debt).
likely_questions: Doctrine of frustration is contained in which section? (56)
Sec 55 time of essence: contract becomes voidable at option of the promisee.
A contingent contract is: collateral event, e.g., insurance contract.

sections.title: Discharge, Breach, Damages and Quasi-Contracts (Secs 62-75)
sections.summary: Damages (Secs 73-74) is the highest-yield topic of the Contract Act, along with novation (Sec 62), restitution (Secs 64-65) and quasi-contract (Secs 68-72).
key_points: Modes of discharge: performance; mutual agreement (novation, rescission, alteration - Sec 62; remission - Sec 63); impossibility (Sec 56); breach; operation of law (insolvency, merger, death in personal contracts); lapse of time (Limitation).

Sec 62 NOVATION: if parties substitute a new contract for the old, or rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed. Novation requires the consent of all parties including the incoming party. Sec 63: a promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promise, or extend the time, or accept any satisfaction (accord and satisfaction) - without fresh consideration. Sec 64: a party who rescinds a voidable contract must restore any benefit he has received. Sec 65: when an agreement is discovered to be void, or a contract becomes void, any person who has received an advantage under it must restore it or make compensation. Sec 66: rescission of voidable contract: may be done by notice. Sec 67: neglect of promisee to afford promisor reasonable facilities for performance excuses the promisor.

Sec 73 DAMAGES: when a contract has been broken, the party who suffers is entitled to compensation for any loss or damage caused to him naturally in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Compensation is NOT given for remote and indirect loss. Explanation: the means of remedying inconvenience must be considered (duty to mitigate). Rule in Hadley v Baxendale (1854): two limbs - natural/ordinary consequences, and special circumstances known to both parties. Damages: compensatory, never punitive. Exemplary damages are generally not awarded for breach of contract, with limited exceptions (breach of promise to marry; wrongful dishonour of a customer's cheque by a bank). Sec 73 also applies to obligations resembling contracts (quasi-contract).

Sec 74 LIQUIDATED DAMAGES & PENALTY: when a contract has been broken, if a sum is named as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Indian law does not distinguish strictly between liquidated damages and penalty - the court awards reasonable compensation (Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das, 1963). The expression 'whether or not actual damage or loss is proved' is subject to: where it is impossible to assess damages, the sum named is a genuine pre-estimate and can be given (ONGC v Saw Pipes, 2003); but where damage is capable of proof, the claimant must prove actual loss (Kailash Nath Associates v DDA, 2015 - forfeiture of earnest money must be reasonable, and if the contract doesn't specify earnest money as security for damages, only the loss proved can be recovered). Forfeiture of earnest money is subject to Sec 74. Sec 74 exception: a stipulation for bail-bond/ recognizance/ similar instrument to the Government (the exception covers bail bonds, bonds to the Government).
Sec 75: a person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for damage sustained through non-fulfilment.

QUASI-CONTRACTS (Secs 68-72) - 'obligations resembling those created by contract': Sec 68: claim for necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting (minor, lunatic) or to his dependants - reimbursement from the property of such person (not personal liability). Sec 69: reimbursement of person paying money due by another in payment of which he is interested. Sec 70: a person lawfully doing anything for another, or delivering anything to him, not intending to act gratuitously, and the other enjoys the benefit, is bound to compensate (State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal, 1962). Conditions: lawful act; not intended to be gratuitous; the other person enjoys the benefit; the other must have the option to accept or reject (Mulamchand v State of MP, 1968 - Sec 70 applies where the contract fails for non-compliance with Art 299). Sec 71: finder of goods - same responsibility as a bailee. Sec 72: a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion must repay or return it (Sales Tax Officer v Kanhaiya Lal Mukund Lal, 1959: refund of tax illegally collected).

Remedies for breach: damages; specific performance; injunction; quantum meruit (Sec 65/70, remuneration for work done where contract is discharged by the other's breach or the contract is void); rescission. Quantum meruit: claim by a party who has partly performed, where the other party prevented completion.

landmark_cases.principle: Remoteness of damage: natural consequence or special knowledge.

landmark_cases.case: Fateh Chand v Balkishan Das (1963)
landmark_cases.principle: Sec 74: reasonable compensation; the party cannot forfeit more than reasonable compensation; the Court can grant relief even if no loss proved up to the named amount.

landmark_cases.case: ONGC v Saw Pipes (2003)
landmark_cases.principle: Liquidated damages enforceable where loss is difficult to assess; Sec 74 and arbitral awards.

landmark_cases.case: Kailash Nath Associates v DDA (2015)
landmark_cases.principle: Forfeiture of earnest money must be proved reasonable; party must show actual loss when quantifiable.

landmark_cases.case: State of West Bengal v B.K. Mondal (1962)
landmark_cases.principle: Sec 70 - benefits enjoyed, no gratuitous intent.

landmark_cases.case: Sales Tax Officer v Kanhaiya Lal Mukund Lal (1959)
landmark_cases.principle: Sec 72 - tax paid under mistake/ coercion refundable.

common_traps: Sec 74 is about reasonable compensation 'not exceeding' the named sum - the sum is a ceiling.
Sec 70 requires the benefit to be ENJOYED - not merely conferred.
Quasi-contract is NOT based on consent; it is based on equity and justice.
Sec 65 applies to void agreements discovered and contracts that become void; Sec 64 to voidable contracts rescinded.
Damages for mental agony: not usually granted in breach of contract (exceptions: marriage promise, hotel booking cases in consumer law).
likely_questions: Sec 73 - remote damages not recoverable; Hadley v Baxendale.
Sec 74 deals with: liquidated damages and penalty.
Sec 72 - money paid by mistake or coercion must be repaid.
Substitution of a new contract for an old one is: novation.

sections.title: Indemnity and Guarantee (Secs 124-147)
sections.summary: A near-certain 1-question area: definitions, distinction, surety's rights, discharge, continuing guarantee.
key_points: Sec 124: contract of indemnity - a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person. (The Act's definition is narrower than English law - covers only loss caused by human conduct, not accidents like fire; but Courts apply equitable principles to other losses.) Sec 125: rights of indemnity-holder: damages he is compelled to pay in a suit; costs; sums paid under compromise. Gajanan Moreshwar Parelkar v Moreshwar Madan Mantri (1942): indemnity-holder may call upon the indemnifier to be relieved of liability before actually paying.

Sec 126: contract of guarantee - a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is the SURETY; the person in respect of whose default it is given is the PRINCIPAL DEBTOR; the person to whom it is given is the CREDITOR. The guarantee may be oral or written.

Three parties; three contracts (principal contract, guarantee, implied contract between surety and principal debtor). In guarantee, there is a primary liability of the principal debtor and secondary liability of the surety. In indemnity, there are two parties and a primary liability of the indemnifier.

Sec 127: anything done, or any promise made, for the benefit of the principal debtor may be a sufficient consideration to the surety. No separate consideration for the surety is needed. Sec 128: the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided (Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad, 1969: creditor may proceed against surety without first suing the principal debtor). Sec 129: continuing guarantee = extends to a series of transactions. Sec 130: continuing guarantee may be revoked as to future transactions by notice to the creditor. Sec 131: death of surety operates as revocation as to future transactions, in the absence of contract to contrary.

Sec 133: any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. Sec 134: the surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and principal debtor by which the principal debtor is released, or by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor. Sec 135: a contract between creditor and principal debtor by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety unless the surety assents. Sec 139: creditor's act or omission impairing the surety's eventual remedy discharges the surety. Sec 136-138: creditor's promise to third person to give time to principal debtor, release of one co-surety does not discharge the other co-sureties.

Sec 140: surety's rights on payment - subrogation to the creditor's rights. Sec 141: surety's right to the benefit of the creditor's securities (even if unaware). Sec 142: guarantee obtained by misrepresentation (by creditor or with his knowledge) is invalid. Sec 143: guarantee obtained by concealment of a material circumstance is invalid. Sec 144: a guarantee given on the condition that the creditor shall not act upon it until another person has joined as co-surety - invalid if that person doesn't join. Sec 145: implied promise by principal debtor to indemnify the surety. Sec 146-147: co-sureties are liable equally (unless contract otherwise) to contribute; where bound in different sums, they contribute equally subject to the maximum limit of each.

Contract of guarantee by a company/bank: bank guarantees are independent of the underlying contract; payment on demand is obligatory except in fraud or irretrievable injustice (U.P. Co-operative Federation v Singh Consultants, 1988). Letters of credit similar.
Banking guarantee note: 'performance guarantee' encashment cannot be injuncted save for fraud/ special equities.

landmark_cases.case: Bank of Bihar v Damodar Prasad (1969)
landmark_cases.principle: Surety's liability is immediate and co-extensive; creditor needn't exhaust remedies against the principal debtor.

landmark_cases.case: Gajanan Moreshwar Parelkar v Moreshwar Madan Mantri (1942)
landmark_cases.principle: Rights of indemnity-holder under Sec 125 are not exhaustive; equitable relief available.

landmark_cases.case: State of Maharashtra v M.N. Kaul (1967)
landmark_cases.principle: Surety discharged where creditor's act (variance) affects principal debtor without his consent.

rows: Indemnifier has no automatic right against third party (unless subrogated)
Surety has right against principal debtor (Sec 140, 145)

common_traps: Sec 128 - co-extensive does not mean identical: the surety's liability may be limited by contract.
Sec 133: variance discharges the surety only for subsequent transactions.
A guarantee for a continuing account - death revokes future liability (Sec 131).
In indemnity, the indemnifier's promise is primary; in guarantee the surety's liability is secondary/collateral.
likely_questions: The liability of a surety is: co-extensive with the principal debtor.
Which section defines contract of guarantee? (126)
Release of principal debtor by creditor: surety discharged (Sec 134).

sections.title: Bailment and Pledge (Secs 148-181)
sections.summary: Definition, duties of bailor/bailee, lien (Sec 170-171), finder (Sec 168-169), pledge and pledgee's right of sale (Sec 176).
key_points: Sec 148: BAILMENT - delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. Person delivering = bailor; person receiving = bailee. Delivery may be actual or constructive (Sec 149). Bailment is based on possession, not ownership; ownership does not pass.

Sec 150: bailor must disclose faults known to him which materially interfere with the use of goods or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks; liable for damage if he fails. In case of bailment for hire, the bailor is responsible even if he did not know of the defects (hire - bailor is liable for faults whether or not known).

Sec 151: duty of care of the bailee - the care which a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. Sec 152: bailee not liable for loss/destruction/deterioration if he has taken the Sec 151 care. Sec 153: bailment terminable at bailor's option if bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions. Sec 154: a bailee making unauthorised use is liable for any damage even if due to unforeseen event. Sec 155-157: mixing of goods - with consent: parties share proportionately; without consent but separable: bailee bears the cost of separation; inseparable: bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss of the goods. Sec 158: bailor's duty to repay necessary expenses. Sec 160: duty to return goods without demand when time expires or purpose accomplished. Sec 161: if bailee fails to return in time, he's responsible for any loss from that time even if not negligent. Sec 163: bailee must deliver to the bailor accretions (increase) in the absence of contract. Sec 164: bailor liable for loss caused to bailee due to defective title.

Sec 168: finder's right to sue for specific reward and to retain the goods until reward. Sec 169: where the owner cannot with reasonable diligence be found, or refuses on demand to pay lawful charges, the finder may sell if (a) the thing is in danger of perishing or losing the greater part of its value, or (b) the lawful charges of the finder in respect of the thing found amount to two-thirds of its value.

Sec 170: BAILEE'S PARTICULAR LIEN - where the bailee has, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, rendered any service involving the exercise of labour or skill in respect of the goods bailed, he has, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, a right to retain such goods until he receives due remuneration. Sec 171: GENERAL LIEN - bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, retain, as security for a general balance of account, any goods bailed to them. Note: only these five categories have general lien.

Sec 172: PLEDGE (pawn) - the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Bailor = pawnor; bailee = pawnee. Sec 173: pawnee's right of retainer; Sec 174: no retention for subsequent advances unless contract; Sec 175: right to extraordinary expenses; Sec 176: where the pawnor makes default, the pawnee may (i) bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt, retaining the goods as collateral, or (ii) sell the thing pledged after giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale; in case of sale, surplus must be paid to the pawnor; deficit remains payable. Sec 177: pawnor's right to redeem at any time before actual sale, on payment of principal, interest and expenses.

Pledge by non-owners: Sec 178 - pledge by a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent is valid if made in the ordinary course of business and the pawnee acts in good faith without notice. Sec 178A: pledge by a person in possession under a voidable contract is valid if the contract has not been rescinded. Sec 179: pledge by a person having a limited interest - valid to the extent of such interest. Sec 180-181: pledge by pawnor/ suit for redemption.
common_traps: Particular lien (Sec 170) is a right of every skilled bailee; general lien (Sec 171) belongs ONLY to bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys, policy-brokers.
Pledge is a species of bailment - requires delivery; pledge of movable only. Mortgage is for immovables.
Finder's right of sale needs perishing or lawful charges >= two-thirds of value.
Bailee's care is the same for gratuitous and non-gratuitous bailments (Sec 151).
likely_questions: General lien is available to: bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys, policy-brokers.
Bailment of goods as security for a debt is: pledge.
Care required of a bailee is: that of a man of ordinary prudence.

sections.title: Agency (Secs 182-238)
sections.summary: Creation of agency, authority, sub-agent, ratification, termination and personal liability of agent are the usual areas.
key_points: Sec 182: agent = a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons; principal = the person for whom such act is done. Sec 183: any person who is of the age of majority and sound mind may employ an agent. Sec 184: as between principal and third persons, any person may become an agent (even a minor), but no person who is not of the age of majority and sound mind shall be responsible to his principal. Sec 185: no consideration is necessary to create an agency.

Sec 186-187: authority may be express (words) or implied (circumstances). Sec 188: an agent having authority to do an act has authority to do every lawful thing necessary to do such act; Sec 189: agent's authority in an emergency to protect the principal from loss (agency of necessity).

Sec 190: an agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts which he has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally, unless by ordinary custom of trade a sub-agent may be employed, or the nature of agency requires. Sec 191: SUB-AGENT = person employed by and acting under the control of the original agent. Sec 192: a properly appointed sub-agent is representing the principal; the agent is responsible to the principal only for his own acts. A substituted agent (Sec 194) is named by the agent and becomes the agent of the principal.

Sec 196: RATIFICATION - where acts are done by one person on behalf of another without his authority, the latter may either ratify or disown them. Ratification may be express or implied (Sec 197). Valid ratification: the act must have been done on behalf of the principal (Sec 196, Keighley Maxsted v Durant); principal must have been in existence and competent at the time of act; with full knowledge of material facts (Sec 198); of the whole transaction (Sec 199); must not injure a third party (Sec 200); cannot be partial or after the lapse of the time within which the act could have been done. A void act (e.g., forgery) cannot be ratified.

Sec 201-210: termination of agency by revocation, renunciation, completion, death or insanity of principal/agent, insolvency of principal, expiry of time, destruction of subject-matter. Sec 202: where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of such interest (AGENCY COUPLED WITH INTEREST - irrevocable). Sec 203: revocation by principal before authority exercised; Sec 205-206: reasonable notice required where the other party would suffer damage. Sec 208: termination takes effect for agent when it becomes known to him; for third persons when it becomes known to them.

Duties of agent (Secs 211-218): conduct business per principal's directions; reasonable skill and diligence (Sec 212); render proper accounts (Sec 213); communicate with the principal (Sec 214); not to deal on own account without consent (Sec 215-216 - principal may repudiate or claim benefit); pay sums received (Sec 218). Principal's duties: indemnify the agent (Sec 222), compensate for neglect (Sec 225), and pay remuneration. Agent's lien: Sec 221.

Personal liability of agent (Sec 230): in the absence of a contract to the contrary, an agent cannot personally enforce, nor be bound by, contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal. Presumption of contract to the contrary: (a) where the contract is made by an agent for the sale or purchase of goods for a merchant resident abroad; (b) where the agent does not disclose the name of his principal; (c) where the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued. Sec 231: unnamed principal; Sec 232-233: option to sue agent or principal (not both - Sec 233: election). Sec 235: person falsely contracting as an agent is liable to the person deceived. Sec 237: principal liable for acts of agent within apparent authority. Sec 238: misrepresentation or fraud by agent within authority binds the principal.
Distinguish: agent vs servant (control test), agent vs independent contractor, agent vs factor/broker. Agent of necessity: Sec 189.
common_traps: Minor can be an agent but is not responsible to his principal (Sec 184); principal must be major and sound minded (Sec 183).
Ratification must be of the whole transaction; a void act cannot be ratified.
Agency coupled with interest is irrevocable and doesn't terminate on the principal's death/insanity (Sec 202, 201).
Sec 185: no consideration needed for agency.
likely_questions: No consideration is necessary to create an agency: Sec 185.
Agency is irrevocable where agent has an interest in the subject-matter: Sec 202.
Sec 230: agent is not personally bound by contract on behalf of principal, with exceptions.

sections.title: Bonus: Sale of Goods Act 1930 and Indian Partnership Act 1932 (low weightage, check syllabus)
sections.summary: Not always asked but sometimes appear in this group. Revise only after finishing core areas.
key_points: SALE OF GOODS ACT: Sec 4 - sale = a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. Sale (executed; property passes) vs agreement to sell (executory; future/ conditional). Goods: all movable property other than actionable claims and money; includes stock, shares, growing crops, grass, things attached to or forming part of land agreed to be severed.

Sec 12: stipulation may be condition (essential to main purpose; breach gives right to repudiate) or warranty (collateral; breach gives only damages). A breach of condition may be treated as breach of warranty (Sec 13). Implied conditions: title (Sec 14(a)), sale by description (Sec 15), quality/fitness (Sec 16 - caveat emptor is the rule with exceptions), merchantability, sale by sample (Sec 17). Implied warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrance (Sec 14(b),(c)).

Passing of property: Sec 18 - specific/ascertained goods needed for transfer; Sec 19 - property passes when parties intend; Sec 20 - specific goods in deliverable state: passes at contract; Sec 23 - unascertained goods: by unconditional appropriation; Sec 24 - sale on approval. Risk follows property (Sec 26) unless otherwise agreed.

Nemo dat quod non habet: Sec 27 - seller cannot give better title than he has. Exceptions: sale by mercantile agent (Sec 27 proviso/ Factors Act), by co-owner in possession (Sec 28), under voidable title (Sec 29), seller or buyer in possession after sale (Sec 30), estoppel, sale by order of court, sale by finder/ pawnee, etc.

Unpaid seller (Sec 45): rights against goods - lien (Sec 47), stoppage in transit (Sec 50), resale (Sec 54); suit for price (Sec 55) and damages for non-acceptance (Sec 56). Buyer's remedies: damages (Sec 57), repudiation, suit for breach of warranty (Sec 59).

PARTNERSHIP ACT: Sec 4 - relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Not status but contract (Sec 5). Mode of determining existence: Sec 6 (real relation; mere sharing of profits is not conclusive). Sec 9: general duties (utmost good faith). Sec 13: rights/duties between partners (interest on capital, remuneration, etc.). Sec 18-19: partner is agent of the firm; implied authority; Sec 19(2) lists acts a partner cannot do under implied authority (e.g., submit disputes to arbitration, open a bank account in own name, compromise claim, withdraw a suit, admit liability, acquire immovable property on behalf of firm - subject to contrary custom). Sec 25: liability of partners joint and several (for all acts of the firm while a partner). Sec 28: holding out (partner by estoppel). Sec 30: minor admitted to the benefits of partnership (no personal liability; may elect to become partner within six months of attaining majority - Sec 30(5)). Sec 32: retirement; Sec 40-44: dissolution; Sec 69: effects of non-registration - an unregistered firm cannot sue (Sec 69(1) - no suit by partner against firm/ other partners; Sec 69(2) - firm against third parties) to enforce a contractual right; but can sue for statutory rights, and can be sued; set-off up to Rs 100 allowed; unregistered status does not affect dissolution suits, receiver actions, etc.
common_traps: Sale of Goods: condition vs warranty - remedies differ.
Partnership: Sec 69 bars suit by unregistered firm for CONTRACTUAL rights; it doesn't invalidate the partnership itself.

sections.title: Overview and the 2018 Amendment
sections.summary: The Specific Relief Act 1963 was substantially amended by the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018 (in force 1 October 2018). Examiners increasingly test post-2018 law: specific performance is now a general rule, not a discretion; substituted performance; infrastructure contracts.
key_points: Sec 4: specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights, not for enforcing penal laws.

Specific relief in the Act: recovery of possession of property (Secs 5-8), specific performance of contracts (Secs 9-25), rectification (Sec 26), rescission (Secs 27-30), cancellation (Secs 31-33), declaratory decrees (Secs 34-35), injunctions (Secs 36-42).

2018 Amendment highlights: (1) Sec 10 - specific performance 'shall' be enforced (earlier 'may be enforced' in the court's discretion; the Sec 20 discretionary clause was repealed and replaced). (2) Sec 14 - rewritten, deleting 'compensation adequate relief' as a ground for refusal. (3) Sec 20 - substituted performance by a third party/ own agency after 30 days' notice. (4) Sec 20A-20C - special provisions for infrastructure project contracts (no injunction; special courts; disposal within 12 months). (5) Sec 21 - compensation in addition to or in substitution, with amendment of plaint allowed. (6) Sec 41(ha) - no injunction impeding infrastructure projects. (7) Sec 16 (personal bars) revised. (8) Secs 6-8 (possession suits) unchanged in substance.

Prospective operation: the Supreme Court has held that the 2018 amendments are substantive and operate prospectively - agreements made before 1 October 2018 are governed by the unamended Act (Katta Sujatha Reddy v Siddamsetty Infra Projects, 2022; recent judgments therefore say 'prior to 2018 amendment'). Be ready for a question distinguishing pre-2018 and post-2018 law.
Sec 9: defences in suits for specific performance are available as in any contract suit - the defendant may plead any ground available under the law relating to contracts.

landmark_cases.case: Katta Sujatha Reddy v Siddamsetty Infra Projects (2022)
landmark_cases.principle: 2018 amendments to SRA are prospective.

common_traps: Post-2018: Specific performance is no longer a discretionary remedy in the old sense; but equitable defences (Sec 16, Sec 14) still limit it.
Pre-2018 contracts: unamended Sec 20 discretion applies.
likely_questions: Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018 came into force on: 1 October 2018.
Which new section introduced 'substituted performance'? Sec 20.
Under the amended Act specific performance is: general rule/ enforceable subject to Secs 11(2), 14, 16.

sections.title: Recovery of Possession (Secs 5-8)
sections.summary: Sec 6 (summary suit for possession) is an AIBE favourite: limitation, no appeal, title irrelevant.
key_points: Sec 5: recovery of specific immovable property - by suit in the manner provided by the CPC (on title).

Sec 6 (SUMMARY SUIT): (1) a person dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law may recover possession by suit, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought (a) after six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree in such suit, nor any review (revision to the High Court is available). (4) Nothing bars a suit to establish title and recover possession.

In a Sec 6 suit, the plaintiff need only prove prior possession and dispossession without consent otherwise than due process; the defendant cannot plead title (jus tertii or his own title). Eviction by due process (decree/execution) is not covered. Sec 6 suit is available also to a tenant against the landlord who evicts him unlawfully, and to a person in settled possession even against the true owner (an owner who takes the law into his hands may be ordered to restore possession).

Sec 7: recovery of specific movable property - a person entitled to the possession may recover it in the manner provided by the CPC. Sec 8: liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to the person entitled to immediate possession - in cases: (a) the thing is held as agent/trustee for the plaintiff; (b) compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (c) it would be extremely difficult to ascertain actual damage; (d) possession has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff.

landmark_cases.case: Nair Service Society v K.C. Alexander (1968)
landmark_cases.principle: Possession is protected against dispossession other than by due process; Sec 6 is a summary remedy.

landmark_cases.case: Sanjay Kumar Pandey v Gulbahar Sheikh (2004)
landmark_cases.principle: Sec 6 suit is to protect settled possession; title not examined; and its scope.

common_traps: Six months limit (not 12 years); no appeal and no review; not against the Government.
A suit under Sec 6 does not bar a later title suit.
likely_questions: Suit under Sec 6 must be brought within: six months.
Is appeal allowed in a Sec 6 suit? No.

sections.title: Specific Performance of Contracts (Secs 9-25)
sections.summary: The heart of the Act. Know what contracts can/cannot be specifically enforced, who can sue, the readiness-and-willingness requirement, and the 2018 reforms.
key_points: Sec 10 (as amended): specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court, subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of Sec 11, Sec 14 and Sec 16.

Sec 11: specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforced - Sec 11(1): where the trustee has contracted within his powers; Sec 11(2): a contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.

Sec 12: specific performance of part of a contract. General rule: court shall not direct specific performance of a part of contract. Exceptions: Sec 12(2): if a party fails to perform a part of the contract which bears only a small proportion to the whole in value and admits of compensation in money, the court may direct specific performance of so much as can be performed and award compensation; Sec 12(3): where a part (of considerable portion) cannot be performed, the court may direct specific performance of the remainder only if the party in default relinquishes all claims to further performance and compensation (or if the plaintiff pays the whole consideration without abatement); Sec 12(4): where a part is separate and distinct, the court can enforce that part.

Sec 13: rights of purchaser or lessee against a person with no title or imperfect title - the buyer can require the seller to make good title acquired subsequently and for compensation, including enforcement against after-acquired title.

Sec 14 (as substituted in 2018): contracts which cannot be specifically enforced: (a) where the party seeking performance has obtained substituted performance under Sec 20; (b) a contract the performance of which involves a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; (d) a contract which in its nature is determinable. Typical examples: contracts of personal service, building contracts requiring continuous supervision, partnership agreements, agreement to marry. Before 2018, additional grounds included contracts where compensation was an adequate relief.
Sec 15: who may obtain specific performance: any party to the contract; representative-in-interest; principal; beneficiary; remainderman; reversioner; the amalgamated company; etc. (Sec 15(a)-(g)).

Sec 16 PERSONAL BARS: specific performance cannot be enforced in favour of a person (a) who has obtained substituted performance under Sec 20; (b) who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that on his part remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with, or in subversion of, the relation intended to be established by the contract; (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant.

READINESS AND WILLINGNESS (Sec 16(c)): 'readiness' = financial capacity to perform (and, where applicable, to produce the money); 'willingness' = conduct/intention. Both must be pleaded and proved, from the date of the agreement until the date of the decree. A plaintiff need not actually tender the price unless the contract so requires (Explanation (ii)), but must show readiness. Delay alone is not fatal if within limitation, but unexplained delay with changing conditions or inconsistent conduct disentitles. Recent Supreme Court judgments of 2026 (Mohammed Khaleel v Jayamma, 23 June 2026; V.N.A.S. Chandran v S. Venila, 31 July 2026) restate this: readiness must be proved by reference to the relevant period, with documentary proof of funds (post-suit FDRs are insufficient), and a decree can be refused after prolonged delay when it would be inequitable. By contrast, the Court has also held that a buyer's delay in issuing a legal notice is not conclusive of lack of willingness where nearly the entire price has been paid (2026 INSC 573).

Sec 17: a contract to sell or let immovable property cannot be specifically enforced in favour of a vendor or lessor who knowingly has no title, or who, though believing he had good title, afterwards becomes aware he has none. Sec 18: where a defendant sets up a variation - the plaintiff can obtain performance only with the variation in cases of fraud/ mistake/ misrepresentation, to produce a legal result, or subsequent variation by parties. Sec 19: relief against parties and persons claiming under them by subsequent title - except a transferee for value who paid money in good faith without notice of the original contract (and a person claiming under a title prior to the contract and known to the plaintiff which might have been displaced by the defendant).

Sec 20 (as substituted in 2018) SUBSTITUTED PERFORMANCE: (1) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of the Contract Act, and subject to the provisions of this section, where the contract is broken due to non-performance of promise by any party, the party who suffers by such breach shall have the option of substituted performance through a third party or by his own agency, and, recover expenses and costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. (2) No substituted performance of contract under sub-section (1) shall be undertaken unless the party who suffers such breach has given a notice in writing, of not less than thirty days, to the party in breach calling upon him to perform the contract within such time as specified in the notice, and on such refusal or failure by the party in breach, the party who suffers such breach may get the same performed by a third party or by his own agency. (3) After the contract has been so performed, the party who suffers such breach shall not be entitled to claim relief of specific performance against the party in breach. (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent the party who has suffered breach of contract from claiming compensation from the party in breach.

Sec 20A: no injunction shall be granted by a court in a suit under this Act involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project specified in the Schedule, where granting the injunction would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of such project. Sec 20B: State Governments, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, to designate special courts (Civil Courts of required grade) to try suits under the Act in respect of infrastructure project contracts. Sec 20C: suits involving infrastructure contracts to be disposed of within twelve months from the date of service of summons to the defendant, extendable by a maximum of six months in total, recorded in writing.

Sec 21: in a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff may also claim compensation for its breach, either in addition to, or in substitution for, such performance; if the court decides that specific performance ought not to be granted, but that there is a contract and the defendant has broken it, and the plaintiff is entitled to compensation, it shall award him compensation; if the court decides that specific performance ought to be granted but that it is insufficient to satisfy the justice of the case, it shall award compensation in addition. If the plaintiff has not claimed compensation, the court shall, at any stage of the proceeding, allow him to amend the plaint. Compensation is assessed under Sec 73 of the Contract Act.

Sec 22: in a suit for specific performance of a contract to transfer immovable property, the plaintiff may also ask for possession, or partition and separate possession, and any other relief, including refund of earnest money/ deposit. Sec 23: a contract that stipulates for payment of liquidated damages in the event of breach does not by itself prevent specific performance, unless the court finds that the intention was that the party in default could pay and be relieved of performance (alternative performance). Sec 24: dismissal of a suit for specific performance bars a suit for compensation for breach, but does not bar other relief to which he is entitled. Sec 25 was omitted by the 2018 Amendment.

Time of essence: time is not of the essence for contracts relating to immovable property unless expressly or impliedly so (Sec 55 Contract Act; Chand Rani v Kamal Rani). Limitation: three years from the date fixed for performance, or if no date, from the date the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused (Article 54, Limitation Act 1963).

Equitable principles that continue to colour the remedy: he who seeks equity must do equity; delay defeats equity; hardship to the defendant; unfair advantage. Post-2018, hardship is only relevant under Sec 20 pre-2018 or as a defence under Sec 9 (e.g. mistake, fraud).

Substituted performance notice period: 30 days.
