sections.title: Rectification, Rescission and Cancellation (Secs 26-33)
sections.summary: Short, bare-act style questions - who can sue, when relief is refused.
key_points: Sec 26 RECTIFICATION: where through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing (not being the articles of association of a company) does not express their real intention, either party (or his representative) may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; the plaintiff may claim rectification in the suit itself. Rectification is available only for a mistake common to both parties (not unilateral); court may rectify and then enforce the contract. Not for the articles of association of a company.

Sec 27 RESCISSION: any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded in cases where (a) the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. Rescission is refused where (a) the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract; (b) owing to change of circumstances (not due to defendant's act) the parties cannot be substantially restored; (c) third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice; (d) the contract is severable and only a part is sought to be rescinded and the part is not severable.

Sec 28: where a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale/lease of immovable property has been passed and the purchaser or lessee does not pay the purchase money or other sum within the period fixed (or extended), the vendor or lessor may apply in the same suit to have the contract rescinded; the court may rescind it for the party in default or altogether. The court has power to extend the time for payment even after the decree (the decree is a preliminary decree in effect).

Sec 29: alternative prayer: in a suit for specific performance, the plaintiff may claim rescission in the alternative. Sec 30: the court may require the party to whom relief is granted to restore benefit received (do equity). Sec 31: CANCELLATION: any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has a reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; the court may order it to be delivered up and cancelled; if the instrument has been registered, the court shall send a copy of the decree to the officer in whose office it has been registered, who shall note on the copy of the instrument the fact of its cancellation. Sec 32: partial cancellation of an instrument. Sec 33: power to require restoration of benefit and compensation.
Limitation: suit to cancel an instrument - three years from when facts entitling cancellation become known (Art 59, Limitation Act).
common_traps: Rectification needs mutual mistake or fraud; not available for articles of association.
Cancellation is for WRITTEN instruments only and needs reasonable apprehension of serious injury.
likely_questions: Rectification of instruments is provided in Sec 26.
Suit for cancellation lies where written instrument is void or voidable (Sec 31).

sections.title: Declaratory Decrees (Secs 34-35)
sections.summary: Sec 34 and its proviso are tested frequently, together with the CPC/limitation angle.
key_points: Sec 34: any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief. PROVISO: no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so.

Essentials: (1) plaintiff is entitled to a legal character or right in property; (2) the defendant has denied or is interested in denying it; (3) the declaration is a matter of judicial discretion; (4) no further relief available which the plaintiff could have asked for. Declaration of status (legal character) - e.g., adoption, legitimacy, marriage. Declaration to be made only against a person denying (not against the whole world).

Declaratory suit for property cases: if plaintiff is not in possession and could seek possession, he must ask for possession (proviso bars bare declaration). If the plaintiff is in possession, a suit for declaration + injunction may be filed. Anathula Sudhakar v P. Buchi Reddy (2008): guidelines - title dispute needs declaration; possession - recovery; injunction suit only for possession.
Sec 35: a declaration is binding only on the parties to the suit, persons claiming through them, and, where the parties are trustees, the persons for whom they are trustees.
Limitation: Article 58 - three years from when the right to sue first accrues.

landmark_cases.case: Anathula Sudhakar v P. Buchi Reddy (2008)
landmark_cases.principle: When a bare injunction suit versus declaration/ possession suits are maintainable; effect of Sec 34 proviso.

common_traps: Sec 34 is DISCRETIONARY; it can be refused even where a right is proved.
A bare declaration of title is barred when possession could have been sought.
likely_questions: Declaration suit proviso: cannot be granted if plaintiff omits further relief available.
Sec 35: effect of declaration binds parties and persons claiming through them.

sections.title: Injunctions (Secs 36-42)
sections.summary: Temporary vs perpetual, mandatory injunction and Sec 41 (when injunction refused) feature almost every year.
key_points: Sec 36: preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual. Sec 37: temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specified time, or until the further order of the court; they may be granted at any stage of a suit and are regulated by the CPC (Order XXXIX). A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit.

Temporary injunction tests (Dalpat Kumar v Prahlad Singh, 1992): (1) prima facie case, (2) balance of convenience, (3) irreparable injury. Interim mandatory injunction is granted rarely and only in a clear case.

Sec 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly or by implication. Where the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in cases such as: the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; there is no standard for ascertaining actual damage; pecuniary compensation would not afford adequate relief; it is probable that compensation cannot be got; or the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of proceedings.

Sec 39: MANDATORY INJUNCTION - when, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts. Sec 40: the plaintiff may claim damages either in addition to or in substitution for an injunction, and damages may be awarded.

Sec 41 WHEN INJUNCTION CANNOT BE GRANTED: (a) to stay a judicial proceeding pending at the institution of the suit unless necessary to prevent multiplicity; (b) to stay proceedings in a court not subordinate to that from which the injunction is sought; (c) to restrain any person from applying to any legislative body; (d) to restrain any person from instituting or prosecuting any proceeding in a criminal matter; (e) to prevent the breach of a contract the performance of which would not be specifically enforced; (f) to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance; (g) to prevent a continuing breach in which the applicant has acquiesced; (h) when equally efficacious relief can certainly be obtained by any other usual mode of proceeding (except in case of breach of trust); (ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facilities (added in 2018); (i) when the conduct of the applicant or his agents has been such as to disentitle him to the assistance of the court; (j) when the applicant has no personal interest in the matter.

Sec 42: where a contract comprises an affirmative agreement to do a certain act, coupled with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do a certain act, the circumstance that the court is unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement shall not preclude it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement, provided that the applicant has not failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him (Lumley v Wagner; Indian application in Niranjan Shankar Golikari).
Limitation for injunction suits: Article 113 (residuary) - three years from when the right to sue accrues; continuing wrong gives a fresh cause each day.

landmark_cases.case: Dalpat Kumar v Prahlad Singh (1992)
landmark_cases.principle: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury.

landmark_cases.case: Lumley v Wagner (1852)
landmark_cases.principle: Negative covenants enforceable by injunction.

common_traps: Sec 41(e): no injunction to prevent breach of contract not specifically enforceable - but Sec 42 is the exception for negative covenants.
Sec 41(d): criminal proceedings cannot be injuncted.
Sec 41(ha) is new in 2018.
likely_questions: Which section lists cases where injunction cannot be granted? Sec 41.
Mandatory injunction: Sec 39.
Perpetual injunction is granted only by decree on merits (Sec 37(2)).

modules.title: Property Law: Transfer of Property Act 1882, Easements Act 1882, Registration Act 1908

sections.title: Transfer of Property Act: General Principles (Secs 1-9)
sections.summary: Definitions and the basic rules of what can be transferred, by whom, and how. Appears in almost every paper.
key_points: Sec 3: immovable property does not include standing timber, growing crops or grass. (General Clauses Act Sec 3(26): land, benefits arising out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth.) 'Attached to the earth' means rooted in the earth (trees, shrubs), imbedded in the earth (walls, buildings), or attached to what is so imbedded for permanent beneficial enjoyment.

Sec 3: a person is said to have NOTICE of a fact when he actually knows it, or when but for wilful abstention from an enquiry or search which he ought to have made, or gross negligence, he would have known it. Constructive notice: registration of a document is notice; possession is notice of the possessor's title.

Sec 5: 'transfer of property' is an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself and one or more other living persons; 'living person' includes a company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not. Hence a transfer to an unborn person is possible only through Sec 13 (trust), and a transfer by will is not a transfer under the Act.

Sec 6: property of any kind may be transferred except: (a) the chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate (spes successionis), the chance of a relation obtaining a legacy on the death of a kinsman, or any other mere possibility of a like nature; (b) a mere right of re-entry for breach of a condition subsequent; (c) an easement apart from the dominant heritage; (d) an interest in property restricted in its enjoyment to the owner personally; (dd) a right to future maintenance, in whatever manner arising, secured, or determined; (e) a mere right to sue; (f) a public office, and the salary of a public officer, whether before or after it has become payable; (g) stipends allowed to military, naval, air-force and civil pensioners of the Government and political pensions; (h) no transfer can be made (1) insofar as it is opposed to the nature of the interest affected thereby, or (2) for an unlawful object or consideration within the meaning of Sec 23 of the Contract Act, or (3) to a person legally disqualified to be transferee; (i) an untransferable interest of an occupancy tenant (subject to law).

Sec 7: every person competent to contract and entitled to transferable property, or authorised to dispose of transferable property not his own, is competent to transfer such property. Sec 8: unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied, a transfer of property passes forthwith to the transferee all the interest which the transferor is then capable of passing, and the legal incidents thereof (including easements, rents, profits, and arrears). Sec 9: a transfer of property may be made without writing in every case in which a writing is not expressly required by law (oral transfers - e.g., sale of tangible immovable property below Rs 100 with delivery of possession, lease for not more than a year, mortgage by deposit of title deeds).

Sec 10: where property is transferred subject to a condition or limitation absolutely restraining the transferee from parting with or disposing of his interest in the property, the condition or limitation is void; exception: lease, where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor or those claiming under him (e.g., no sub-letting). Sec 11: where, on a transfer of property, an interest therein is created absolutely in favour of any person, but the transferee is directed to deal with the interest in a particular manner for the benefit of another, the transferee takes the interest free of the direction, unless there is a legal obligation (not applied where there is an obligation in the nature of a trust). Sec 12: condition that the transfer shall cease to have effect if the transferee becomes insolvent or attempts to alienate is void (not applicable to lessee for the benefit of the lessor).

Sec 13: where on a transfer of property an interest therein is created for the benefit of a person not in existence at the date of the transfer, subject to a prior interest created by the same transfer, the interest created for the benefit of such person shall not take effect, unless it extends to the whole of the remaining interest of the transferor in the property. Sec 14: RULE AGAINST PERPETUITIES - no transfer of property can operate to create an interest which is to take effect after the life-time of one or more persons living at the date of such transfer, and the minority of some person who shall be in existence at the expiration of that period, and to whom, if he attains full age, the interest created is to belong. In effect: the vesting must be within a life in being + minority (18 years). Sec 15: transfer to a class some of whom cannot take; Sec 16: transfer to take effect on failure of prior transfer; Sec 17: direction for accumulation - void beyond life of the transferor, or 18 years from the date of transfer, whichever is shorter; Sec 18: perpetuity exception in favour of the public (charities).

Vested and contingent interests: Sec 19 - a vested interest is created in favour of a person without reference to the time of enjoyment; Sec 20 - unborn person acquires vested interest on birth; Sec 21 - contingent interest depends on a specified uncertain event; Sec 22 - transfer to members of a class; Secs 23-34 - conditional transfers and conditions precedent/ subsequent: Sec 25 - an interest created on a condition that is impossible, unlawful or immoral is void; Sec 31 - an interest created on transfer for the benefit of any person, but which is to cease on a specified uncertain event, is valid if the condition is not illegal.
common_traps: Spes successionis (chance of succession) is NOT transferable. Mere right to sue is NOT transferable (but a right to sue for specific property or for money due is transferable as an actionable claim).
Right to future maintenance is not transferable; arrears of maintenance are.
Sec 10 restraint on alienation is void - but partial restraints (time-bound or limited to class) may be valid. Lease restraints in favour of lessor are valid.
Perpetuity: life in being + minority period (18 years).
likely_questions: Which of the following cannot be transferred under Sec 6? spes successionis / mere right to sue / public office / personal easement.
Rule against perpetuities is in Sec 14.
Sec 5 defines transfer of property: between living persons.

sections.title: Doctrines under the TPA (Election, Ostensible Owner, Estoppel, Lis Pendens, Part Performance)
sections.summary: Sections 35, 41, 43, 52, 53, 53A are the most frequently tested doctrinal provisions.
key_points: Sec 35 ELECTION: where a person professes to transfer property which he has no right to transfer, and as part of the same transaction confers any benefit on the owner of the property, such owner must elect either to confirm such transfer or to dissent from it; and, in the latter case, he shall relinquish the benefit so conferred, and the benefit so relinquished reverts to the transferor or his representative as if it had not been disposed of, subject to the charge of making good to the disappointed transferee the amount or value of the property attempted to be transferred to him. Based on the maxim: 'he who accepts a benefit under an instrument must adopt the whole.' Election arises only from a single transaction; the elector must have knowledge of the facts and the right to elect.

Sec 41 OSTENSIBLE OWNER: where, with the consent, express or implied, of the persons interested in immovable property, a person is the ostensible owner of such property and transfers the same for consideration, the transfer shall not be voidable on the ground that the transferor was not authorised to make it, provided that the transferee, after taking reasonable care to ascertain that the transferor had power to make the transfer, has acted in good faith. Conditions: (1) ostensible ownership; (2) consent of real owner (express or implied); (3) transfer for consideration; (4) transferee's good faith and reasonable care. Applies only to immovable property; real owner's omission or willful absence from interference is implied consent (Ram Coomar Coondoo; Ramcoomar v Macqueen; and the leading modern case Jayadayal Poddar v Bibi Hazra, 1974 - burden on transferee).

Sec 43 FEEDING THE GRANT BY ESTOPPEL: where a person fraudulently or erroneously represents that he is authorised to transfer certain immovable property and professes to transfer such property for consideration, such transfer shall, at the option of the transferee, operate on any interest which the transferor may acquire in such property at any time during which the contract of transfer subsists. Proviso: nothing in this section shall impair the right of transferees in good faith for consideration without notice of the existence of the said option. The transfer operates on the after-acquired interest (the grantor's subsequently acquired title 'feeds' the earlier grant). The transferee must not have had knowledge of the transferor's lack of title (a transferee with knowledge cannot invoke Sec 43). Distinguish from Sec 41: Sec 41 protects against the OWNER; Sec 43 enforces against the TRANSFEROR's subsequently acquired interest.

Sec 51: improvements by bona fide holder under defective title - the transferee who makes improvements believing in good faith that he is absolutely entitled is entitled to compensation, or to have the improvements removed, on eviction by the person having a better title. Sec 52 LIS PENDENS: during the pendency in any court having authority within the limits of India of a suit or proceeding which is not collusive and in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the court and on such terms as it may impose. Based on the maxim pendente lite nihil innovetur. Lis pendens operates as a rule of public policy irrespective of notice; the transfer is not void but subordinate to the decree (it is 'subject to the outcome'). The transferee pendente lite may be impleaded and is bound by the decree. The lis commences with the presentation of the plaint and continues until final disposal and satisfaction of the decree. 'Right to immovable property directly and specifically in question': suits for partition, redemption, specific performance of sale, title.

Sec 53 FRAUDULENT TRANSFER: (1) every transfer of immovable property made with intent to defeat or delay the creditors of the transferor shall be voidable at the option of any creditor so defeated or delayed. Nothing shall impair the rights of a transferee in good faith and for consideration. (2) Every transfer of immovable property made without consideration with intent to defraud a subsequent transferee shall be voidable at the option of such transferee. The transferee in good faith and for consideration is protected. The suit by a creditor shall be instituted on behalf of or for the benefit of all the creditors (Sec 53(1) explanation). Intention of the transferor to defraud is the key (Twyne's case, 1601). Benami transactions are separately regulated.

Sec 53A PART PERFORMANCE: where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing signed by him or on his behalf from which the terms necessary to constitute the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, and the transferee has, in part performance of the contract, taken possession of the property or any part thereof, or the transferee, being already in possession, continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance of the contract, and has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract, then, notwithstanding that the contract, though required to be registered, has not been registered, or, where there is an instrument of transfer, that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefor by the law for the time being in force, the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract. Essential conditions: (i) written contract signed by the transferor, with ascertainable terms; (ii) transferee took/continued possession in part performance; (iii) transferee did some act in furtherance; (iv) transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part. It is a SHIELD (a defence), not a SWORD - the transferee cannot sue for title on the basis of Sec 53A alone (Ghantesher Ghosh v Madan Mohan Ghosh, 1996 - principle; Delhi Motor Co v U.A. Basrurkar, 1968; Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi, 2002). After the 2001 amendment (Act 48 of 2001), the contract must be REGISTERED under Registration Act Sec 17(1A) to claim Sec 53A protection for contracts executed on or after 24 January 2001; unregistered agreements to sell cannot be relied upon for Sec 53A.

Sec 48: where a person purports to create by transfer at different times rights in or over the same immovable property, and such rights cannot all exist or be exercised to their full extent together, each later right shall, in the absence of a special contract or reservation binding the earlier transferees, be subject to the rights previously created (priority - 'qui prior est tempore potior est jure'). Sec 50: rent; Sec 44: transfer by one co-owner - the transferee acquires the transferor's share and has the right to joint possession/ partition.

GPA/ SA/ WILL transactions: Suraj Lamp & Industries v State of Haryana (2012) - immovable property can be legally and lawfully transferred or conveyed only by a registered deed of conveyance; transactions of sale through agreement to sell, general power of attorney, and will (SA/GPA/WILL) do not convey title or create any interest in an immovable property; they may only be treated as agreement to sell and Sec 53A protection (if registered). This ruling is prospective for completed transactions but, going forward, binding. A power of attorney is not an instrument of transfer.

sections.title: Sale of Immovable Property (Secs 54-57)
sections.summary: Mode of sale, rights and liabilities of seller and buyer, seller's charge. Nearly guaranteed.
key_points: Sec 54: 'sale' is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised. Such transfer, in the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument. In the case of tangible immovable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, such transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property. Delivery of tangible immovable property takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as he directs, in possession of the property.

Contract for sale (agreement to sell): a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties. It does NOT, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property (Sec 54, last para). Hence a purchaser under an agreement to sell has no title; he has only a right to sue for specific performance (and Sec 53A protection if the conditions are satisfied).

Sec 55(1) SELLER'S DUTIES: (a) to disclose to the buyer any material defect in the property or in the seller's title of which the seller is, and the buyer is not, aware, and which the buyer could not with ordinary care discover; (b) to produce to the buyer on his request for examination all documents of title relating to the property which are in the seller's possession or power; (c) to answer to the best of his information all relevant questions put to him by the buyer in respect to the property or the title thereto; (d) on payment or tender of the amount due in respect of the price, to execute a proper conveyance of the property when the buyer tenders it to him for execution at a proper time and place; (e) between the date of the contract of sale and the delivery of the property, to take as much care of the property and all documents of title relating thereto which are in his possession as an owner of ordinary prudence would take of such property and documents; (f) to give, on being so required, the buyer, or such person as he directs, such possession of the property as its nature admits; (g) to pay all public charges and rents accrued due in respect of the property up to the date of the sale, the interest on all encumbrances on such property due on such date, and, except where the property is sold subject to encumbrances, to discharge all encumbrances on the property then existing.

Sec 55(2): the seller is deemed to contract with the buyer that the interest which the seller professes to transfer subsists and that he has power to transfer the same (implied covenant for title); in a sale of a mortgage, etc., different. Sec 55(3): where the whole or any part of the purchase-money has been paid to the seller by the buyer before the sale is complete (i.e., on or before execution) the buyer is entitled to a charge. Sec 55(4): SELLER'S CHARGE - the seller is entitled to a charge upon the property, as against the buyer and all persons claiming under him, for the amount of the purchase-money, or any part thereof remaining unpaid, and for interest on such amount or part from the date on which possession is delivered. Seller's charge is lost if the seller has given up possession or by agreement; it is enforceable against transferees with notice.

Sec 55(5) BUYER'S DUTIES: (a) to disclose to the seller any fact as to the nature or extent of the seller's interest in the property of which the buyer is aware, but of which he has reason to believe that the seller is not aware, and which materially increases the value of such interest; (b) to pay or tender, at the time and place of completing the sale, the purchase-money to the seller or such person as he directs - the buyer's tender of the price at the proper time; (c) where the ownership of the property has passed to the buyer before payment of the whole of the purchase-money, to pay interest on the unpaid purchase-money from the date of passing ownership; (d) as between the seller and buyer, after the ownership of the property has passed to the buyer, to bear any loss arising from the destruction, injury or decrease in value of the property not caused by the seller, and to pay all public charges and rents which become payable in respect of the property after the date of the sale.

Sec 55(6)(b): the buyer is entitled to the benefit of any improvement in, or increase in value of, the property, and the rents and profits thereof, from the date on which the ownership is passed to him. Sec 55(6)(b) buyer's charge: a charge on the property, as against the seller and all persons claiming under him, to the extent of the seller's interest in the property, for the amount of any purchase-money properly paid by the buyer in anticipation of the delivery of possession and for interest on such amount; and, when he properly declines to accept the delivery of the property for any improper cause, for the earnest (if any) and costs awarded to him of a suit to compel specific performance. The charge arises by operation of law.

Sec 56: marshalling by subsequent purchaser - if the owner of two or more properties mortgages them to one person and then sells one or more to another person, the buyer is, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, entitled to have the mortgage debt satisfied out of the property or properties not sold to him, so far as the same will extend, but not so as to prejudice the rights of the mortgagee or persons claiming under him. Sec 57: sale of mortgaged property by court - rights of buyer on a Court sale.

Registration: sale of immovable property requires registration under the Registration Act 1908 (Sec 17(1)(b)); the document is also required to be stamped. An unregistered sale deed cannot convey title (except for tangible property < Rs 100 with delivery of possession); it is inadmissible in evidence to prove the transaction except for the limited collateral purposes (Registration Act Sec 49).

Sale of property in execution of a decree: the Civil Procedure Code (Order XXI) and Sec 54 do not apply to court sales for mode of transfer. A sale certificate is deemed a transfer of title at the date of the confirmation of sale (Order XXI Rule 94).
common_traps: Sale of tangible immovable property worth Rs 100 and above: ONLY by registered instrument; below Rs 100 - registered instrument OR delivery of possession.
Agreement to sell does NOT create any interest in or charge on the property.
Seller's charge (Sec 55(4)) arises for unpaid price with interest from date of delivery of possession.
Buyer bears the loss after ownership has passed (Sec 55(5)(d)).
likely_questions: Sale of tangible immovable property of Rs 100 and above requires: registered instrument.
Contract for sale: does not by itself create any interest in the property.
Seller's charge for unpaid purchase money: Sec 55(4).

sections.title: Mortgage (Secs 58-104)
sections.summary: The single most important chapter of the TPA. Expect questions on definition, the six types, mode of creation (Sec 59), redemption (Sec 60), foreclosure and sale (Sec 67), mortgagee-in-possession and priority.
key_points: Sec 58(a): a mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. The transferor is called the mortgagor, the transferee a mortgagee; the principal money and interest of which payment is secured for the time being are called the mortgage-money, and the instrument (if any) by which the transfer is effected is called a mortgage-deed. A mortgage is a transfer of an INTEREST (not ownership); the mortgagor retains the equity of redemption.

Sec 58(b) SIMPLE MORTGAGE: without delivering possession of the mortgaged property, the mortgagor binds himself personally to pay the mortgage-money, and agrees, expressly or impliedly, that, in the event of his failing to pay according to his contract, the mortgagee shall have a right to cause the mortgaged property to be sold and the proceeds of sale to be applied, so far as may be necessary, in payment of the mortgage-money. REMEDY: suit for sale (Sec 67); personal remedy. Possession remains with mortgagor.

Sec 58(c) MORTGAGE BY CONDITIONAL SALE: the mortgagor ostensibly sells the mortgaged property (i) on condition that on default of payment of the mortgage-money on a certain date the sale shall become absolute, or (ii) on condition that on such payment being made the sale shall become void, or (iii) on condition that on such payment being made the buyer shall transfer the property to the seller. Proviso: no such transaction shall be deemed to be a mortgage, unless the condition is embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale. REMEDY: foreclosure (Sec 67). Distinguish from a sale with a condition of repurchase (a separate document or a contemporaneous contract would be a sale with option to repurchase, not a mortgage).

Sec 58(d) USUFRUCTUARY MORTGAGE: the mortgagor delivers possession or expressly or by implication binds himself to deliver possession of the mortgaged property to the mortgagee, and authorises him to retain such possession until payment of the mortgage-money, and to receive the rents and profits accruing from the property or any part of such rents and profits and to appropriate the same in lieu of interest, or in payment of the mortgage-money, or partly in lieu of interest or partly in payment of the mortgage-money. REMEDY: retention of possession until the debt is satisfied; no right to foreclose or sell (unless the deed provides in addition); no personal liability unless the mortgagor has so covenanted. Mortgagor's right: recover possession on payment or on the rents and profits discharging the debt (Sec 62).

Sec 58(e) ENGLISH MORTGAGE: the mortgagor binds himself to repay the mortgage-money on a certain date, and transfers the mortgaged property absolutely to the mortgagee, but subject to a proviso that he will re-transfer it to the mortgagor upon payment of the mortgage-money as agreed. Features: absolute transfer + personal covenant + re-transfer proviso. Sec 69: power of sale without court intervention is available to an English mortgagee in specified places (where the mortgagor and mortgagee are Hindu, Muslim, Buddhist - excluded in some towns - and where the mortgagee is the Government), subject to notice and conditions. Sec 58(f) EQUITABLE MORTGAGE (MORTGAGE BY DEPOSIT OF TITLE-DEEDS): where a person in any of the towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay, and in any other town which the State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify, delivers to a creditor or his agent documents of title to immovable property, with intent to create a security thereon, the transaction is called a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds. Requires: (i) a debt; (ii) deposit of title-deeds; (iii) intention to create security. No writing or registration is required (Sec 59 exempts). If a memorandum of deposit is executed that itself creates the mortgage, it needs registration. REMEDY: sale (and foreclosure not available); personal liability if there is a covenant. Sec 58(g) ANOMALOUS MORTGAGE: a mortgage which is not a simple mortgage, a mortgage by conditional sale, an usufructuary mortgage, an English mortgage or a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds within the meaning of this section.

Sec 59: where the principal money secured is one hundred rupees or upwards, a mortgage can be effected only by a registered instrument signed by the mortgagor and attested by at least two witnesses. Where the principal money secured is less than one hundred rupees, a mortgage may be effected either by a registered instrument signed and attested as aforesaid, or (except in the case of a simple mortgage) by delivery of the property. Mortgage by deposit of title-deeds is excepted. A mortgage not attested by two witnesses is invalid as a mortgage (not saved by Sec 59 later amendment). Attestation requires the witness to see the executant sign (Sec 3 TPA 'attested').

Sec 60 RIGHT TO REDEEM: at any time after the principal money has become payable, the mortgagor has a right, on payment or tender, at a proper time and place, of the mortgage-money, to require the mortgagee (a) to deliver to the mortgagor the mortgage-deed and all documents relating to the mortgaged property which are in the possession or power of the mortgagee; (b) where the mortgagee is in possession of the mortgaged property, to deliver possession thereof to the mortgagor; (c) at the cost of the mortgagor either to re-transfer the mortgaged property to him or to such third person as he may direct, or to execute and (where the mortgage has been effected by a registered instrument) to have registered an acknowledgment in writing that any right in derogation of his interest transferred to the mortgagee has been extinguished. The right conferred is called a right to redeem, and a suit to enforce it is a suit for redemption. The right of redemption is not extinguished except by the act of the parties or by decree of a court. The CLOG ON EQUITY OF REDEMPTION rule - 'once a mortgage always a mortgage': any stipulation that restricts or fetters the right of redemption (e.g., condition postponing redemption for an unreasonable time or giving the mortgagee a collateral advantage) is void (Seth Ganga Dhar v Shankar Lal, 1958; Noakes & Co v Rice). Sec 60A: mortgagor's right to require assignment instead of re-transfer. Sec 61: right to redeem separately or simultaneously where mortgagor has executed two or more mortgages in favour of the same mortgagee (consolidation of mortgages is permitted only where the mortgages contain such a condition).

Sec 62: usufructuary mortgagor's right to recover possession - on the mortgagee's receipt of rents and profits satisfying the principal and interest, or on payment of the remaining sum or deposit; Sec 63: accession to mortgaged property - in the absence of contract, the mortgagee in possession is entitled to the accession; Sec 63A: improvements to mortgaged property; Sec 65: mortgagor's rights while in possession; Sec 65A: MORTGAGOR'S POWER TO LEASE - a mortgagor in possession may lease the property: agricultural lease for a term not exceeding 5 years; non-agricultural lease (house, etc.) not exceeding 3 years; the lease must take effect from a date not later than six months from the date on which it is made, reserve the best rent obtainable, without premium and without payment of rent in advance, and not contain a covenant for renewal. Sec 66: mortgagor's waste (a mortgagor in possession must not commit acts destructive or permanently injurious to the property).

Sec 67: RIGHT TO FORECLOSE OR SELL - at any time after the mortgage-money has become due to him, and before a decree has been made for the redemption of the mortgaged property, or the mortgage-money has been paid or deposited as hereinafter provided, the mortgagee has, subject to the provisions of Sec 67A, a right to obtain from the Court an order that the mortgagor shall be absolutely debarred of his right to redeem the property (a decree for foreclosure), or an order that the property be sold (a decree for sale). Foreclosure is available only in mortgage by conditional sale and in anomalous mortgage if the deed so provides; sale is available in simple, English (but English mortgagee can sell only by court unless Sec 69), equitable (deposit of title deeds) mortgages. Usufructuary mortgagee: neither foreclosure nor sale (unless deed provides otherwise). Sec 68: right to sue for the mortgage-money - only in cases where the mortgagor binds himself to repay, or where the mortgagee is deprived of possession/ security is destroyed, or where the mortgagee is entitled to possession but the mortgagor fails to deliver. Sec 69: power of sale without intervention of the court (only for English mortgages and for mortgages in which the deed gives a power of sale - to be exercised after notice and 3 months' default, and subject to the limitations in Sec 69); Sec 69A: power to appoint receiver.

Sec 70: accession to mortgaged property; Sec 72: rights of mortgagee in possession - to spend money necessary for the preservation of the property, defend title, protect from forfeiture; Sec 73: charge on proceeds of insurance and on the compensation (acquired under the Land Acquisition law); Sec 76: LIABILITIES OF MORTGAGEE IN POSSESSION - (a) to manage the property as a person of ordinary prudence would manage; (b) to use his best endeavours to collect the rents and profits; (c) to apply the receipts in due order; (d) to keep accounts; (e) not to commit waste; and he is liable for loss due to his wilful default or gross negligence. Sec 77: receipts in lieu of interest. Sec 78: POSTPONEMENT OF PRIOR MORTGAGEE - where, through the fraud, misrepresentation or gross neglect of a prior mortgagee, another person has been induced to advance money on the security of the mortgaged property, the prior mortgagee shall be postponed to the subsequent mortgagee (e.g., leaving title deeds with the mortgagor). Sec 79: mesne mortgagee has the same rights against prior and subsequent mortgagees as a mortgagee. Sec 81: marshalling securities - if the owner of two or more properties mortgages them to one person and then mortgages one or more of the properties to another person, the subsequent mortgagee is, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, entitled to have the prior mortgage-debt satisfied out of the property or properties not mortgaged to him. Sec 82: contribution to mortgage-debt where properties of different persons are mortgaged. Sec 83: deposit in court by mortgagor - mortgagor may deposit the amount due in court and the interest ceases from the date of deposit.

Sec 85: all persons having an interest in the property or the right of redemption (mortgagor/ subsequent mortgagees/ transferees) must be joined as parties in suits for foreclosure, sale and redemption (Order XXXIV CPC); Sec 88-90: preliminary and final decrees; Sec 90 (deficiency decree): if the sale proceeds are insufficient the mortgagee may obtain personal decree for the balance (Order XXXIV Rule 6 CPC). Sec 91: persons who may sue for redemption: any person (other than the mortgagee of the interest sought to be redeemed) who has any interest in, or charge upon, the property mortgaged or in or upon the right to redeem the same, or any surety for the payment of the mortgage-debt or any part thereof. Sec 92: SUBROGATION - any of the persons referred to in Sec 91 (other than the mortgagor), and any co-mortgagor, shall, on redeeming property subject to the mortgage, have, so far as regards the redemption, foreclosure or sale of such property, the same rights as the mortgagee whose mortgage he redeems. Sec 93-96: Sec 94 priority of a person redeeming (not necessary here).

Limitation (Limitation Act 1963): suit by mortgagor to redeem - 30 years from when the right to redeem or to recover possession accrues (Article 61(a)); suit by mortgagee for foreclosure - 30 years from the date the money sued for becomes due (Article 63(a)); suit by mortgagee for possession of the property mortgaged - 12 years from the date of the mortgage-money becoming due (Article 63(b)); suit to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage or charged upon immovable property (sale) - 12 years from when the money sued for becomes due (Article 62).

Recent trend: SARFAESI Act and IBC lawyers - mortgages enforced extra-judicially by banks under SARFAESI Sec 13; Sec 69 TPA power of sale. Also: registration of mortgage by deposit of title deeds - banks register memorandum/ CERSAI registration (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest) for creation of security interest.

landmark_cases.case: Seth Ganga Dhar v Shankar Lal (1958)
landmark_cases.principle: Clog on equity of redemption - any fetter on the right to redeem is void.

common_traps: Foreclosure is available ONLY for mortgage by conditional sale (and anomalous if so provided).
Equitable mortgage requires: deposit of title deeds in a notified town with the intention to create security; no writing or registration necessary.
Mortgage of Rs 100 and above requires a registered instrument signed by the mortgagor and attested by 2 witnesses.
Mortgagor's lease power under Sec 65A: agricultural up to 5 years; non-agricultural up to 3 years.
Right of redemption cannot be fettered - clog on equity of redemption.
Usufructuary mortgagee cannot foreclose or sue for sale.
likely_questions: Mortgage by deposit of title-deeds: Sec 58(f).
Which mortgage gives right of foreclosure? Mortgage by conditional sale.
Mortgagee's right to foreclose or sell: Sec 67.
Right to redeem: Sec 60; subrogation: Sec 92; marshalling: Sec 81.
Mortgage of Rs 100 and above: registered instrument, 2 attesting witnesses.

sections.title: Charge (Sec 100)
sections.summary: A short but frequently tested concept: charge vs mortgage.
key_points: Sec 100: where immovable property of one person is by act of parties or operation of law made security for the payment of money to another, and the transaction does not amount to a mortgage, the latter person is said to have a charge on the property; and all the provisions hereinbefore contained which apply to a simple mortgage shall, so far as may be, apply to such charge. A charge is created by (a) act of parties - e.g., a document creating a charge for maintenance, marriage expenses; or (b) operation of law - e.g., seller's charge (Sec 55(4)(b)), buyer's charge (Sec 55(6)(b)), charge of the mortgagor on insurance proceeds, Sec 73, partner's charge, etc.

A charge does not transfer an interest in the property; a mortgage does. A charge is enforceable against any person who takes the property with notice (except a transferee for consideration without notice, Sec 100 proviso: 'no charge shall be enforced against any property in the hands of a person to whom such property has been transferred for consideration and without notice of the charge'). A charge created by act of parties needs registration if the amount is Rs 100 or more. A charge may be created by will (a charge on the testator's property for legacies).

Distinction: a mortgage = transfer of interest; a charge = security without transfer of interest; mortgage can only be created by act of parties; a charge by act of parties or by operation of law; mortgage can be of immovable property only; charge can be of immovable or movable property in other statutes (floating charge under the Companies Act); mortgage confers a right to foreclose in some cases (not charge); charge is enforceable only by sale (as simple mortgage).
common_traps: Charge is NOT a transfer of interest in property; mortgage is.
Charge cannot be enforced against a bona fide transferee for value without notice.
likely_questions: A charge may be created by: act of parties or operation of law.
Seller's charge is a charge by operation of law.

sections.title: Lease (Secs 105-117)
sections.summary: Definition, formalities, duration (Sec 106), lessor/lessee rights, determination (Sec 111), forfeiture and holding over are recurring topics; lease vs licence is a perennial favourite.
key_points: Sec 105: a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee, who accepts the transfer on such terms. Transferor = lessor; transferee = lessee; the price = premium; the money, share, service or other thing = rent.

Essentials of a lease: (1) parties competent; (2) subject-matter - immovable property; (3) transfer of a right to enjoy (not ownership), i.e., exclusive possession; (4) for a certain time or in perpetuity; (5) consideration - premium or rent; (6) acceptance by lessee. A lease is a transfer of an INTEREST in property (it creates an estate); a LICENCE (Easements Act Sec 52) merely makes lawful what would otherwise be unlawful and creates no interest. The test is whether the document gives exclusive possession and an interest (intention of the parties) - Associated Hotels of India v R.N. Kapoor (1959); Sohan Lal v Union of India (1957).

Sec 106: DURATION - in the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice (amended in 2002). Such notice must be in writing, signed by or on behalf of the person giving it, and either sent by post to the party who is intended to be bound by it or tendered or delivered personally to such party, or to one of his family or servants at his residence, or (if such tender or delivery is not practicable) affixed to a conspicuous part of the property. After the 2002 amendment the notice period for a monthly tenancy is fifteen days.

Sec 107: A lease of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent, can be made only by a registered instrument. All other leases of immovable property may be made either by a registered instrument or by oral agreement accompanied by delivery of possession. Where a lease of immovable property is made by a registered instrument, such instrument or, where there are more instruments than one, each such instrument shall be executed by both the lessor and the lessee (Sec 107 proviso - the State Government may exempt leases not exceeding 3 years). An unregistered lease for more than one year is invalid as a lease but may be evidence of the nature of possession (a tenancy from year to year or month to month may be implied by acceptance of rent and possession - Sec 116 and Anthony v K.C. Ittoop & Sons, 2000: it is a tenancy from year to year/ month to month; the unregistered deed is admissible for collateral purposes).

Sec 108 RIGHTS AND LIABILITIES: Lessor: (a) to disclose to the lessee any material defect in the property, with reference to its intended use, of which the lessor is and the lessee is not aware, and which the lessee could not with ordinary care discover; (b) to put the lessee in possession of the property on his request; (c) QUIET ENJOYMENT - the lessor is deemed to contract with the lessee that, if the lessee pays the rent reserved and performs the contracts binding on the lessee, he may hold the property during the time limited by the lease without interruption. Lessee: (d) to disclose facts as to the nature or extent of the interest which the lessee is about to take of which the lessee is, and the lessor is not, aware, and which materially increase the value of such interest; (e) rent - to pay or tender, at the proper time and place, the premium or rent; (f) to keep the property in good condition; (g) the lessee may remove, at any time during the continuance of the lease, all things which he has attached to the earth, provided he leaves the property in the state in which he received it; (h) the lessee may transfer absolutely or by way of mortgage or sub-lease the whole or any part of his interest in the property, and any transferee of such interest or part may again transfer it (the lessee remains liable to the lessor under the lease); the lessee must not commit waste, must protect the property from injury, and on determination of the lease must put the lessor into possession. The lessee is entitled to the benefit of any accession to the property during the term.

Sec 109: if the lessor transfers the property leased, or any part thereof, or any part of his interest therein, the transferee, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, shall possess all the rights, and, if the lessee so elects, be subject to all the liabilities of the lessor as to the property or part transferred so long as he is the owner of it (the transferee can sue the lessee for rent; the lessee can attorn). Sec 110: exclusion of day on which term commences - where the time limited by a lease of immovable property is expressed as commencing from a particular day, the day is to be excluded; and where it is expressed as ending on a particular day, that day is included in the term.

Sec 111 DETERMINATION OF LEASE: (a) by efflux of the time limited thereby; (b) where such time is limited conditionally on the happening of some event - by the happening of such event; (c) where the interest of the lessor in the property terminates on, or his power to dispose of the same extends only to, the happening of any event - by the happening of such event; (d) where the interest of the lessee and the interest of the lessor in the whole of the property become vested at the same time in one person in the same right (merger); (e) by express surrender, i.e., in case the lessee yields up his interest under the lease to the lessor, by mutual agreement between them; (f) by implied surrender; (g) by forfeiture - (1) in case the lessee breaks an express condition which provides that, on breach thereof, the lessor may re-enter; or (2) in case the lessee renounces his character as such by setting up a title in a third person or by claiming title in himself; or (3) the lessee is adjudicated an insolvent and the lease provides that the lessor may re-enter on the happening of such event; and in any of these cases the lessor or his transferee gives notice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease; (h) on the expiration of a notice to determine the lease, or to quit, or of intention to quit, the property leased, duly given by one party to the other (notice to quit).

Sec 112: waiver of forfeiture - a forfeiture under Sec 111(g) is waived by acceptance of rent which has become due since the forfeiture, or by distress for such rent, or by any other act on the part of the lessor showing an intention to treat the lease as subsisting. Sec 113: waiver of notice to quit - a notice given under Sec 111(h) is waived, with the express or implied consent of the person to whom it is given, by any act on the part of the person giving it showing an intention to treat the lease as subsisting. Sec 114: relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent - where a lease of immovable property has been determined by forfeiture for non-payment of rent, and the lessor sues to eject the lessee, if, at the hearing of the suit, the lessee pays or tenders to the lessor the rent in arrear, together with interest thereon and his full costs of the suit, or gives security to the satisfaction of the Court for payment of such rent, interest and costs, the Court may, in lieu of making a decree for ejectment, pass an order relieving the lessee against the forfeiture. Sec 114A: relief against forfeiture in certain other cases - notice of the breach is required to be given to the lessee (not applicable to breach of express condition against assigning, under-letting, etc.). Sec 115: effect of notice to determine lease. Sec 116: EFFECT OF HOLDING OVER - if a lessee or under-lessee of property remains in possession thereof after the determination of the lease granted to the lessee, and the lessor or his legal representative accepts rent from the lessee or under-lessee, or otherwise assents to his continuing in possession, the lease is, in the absence of an agreement to the contrary, renewed from year to year, or from month to month, according to the purpose for which the property is leased, as specified in Sec 106 (a tenancy by holding over is a new tenancy, not an extension). Sec 117: exemption of leases for agricultural purposes - none of the provisions of Secs 105 to 116 apply to leases for agricultural purposes, except in so far as the State Government may by notification in the Official Gazette so direct.

A lessee has an interest - heritable and transferable; the lease isn't terminated by the death of lessor or lessee. Eviction under rent control legislation: tenant protections override Sec 106 in many States (so a lease determined by notice to quit may still require a statutory ground for eviction; the 'statutory tenant' is entitled to remain). Rent Acts: the Model Tenancy Act 2021 (Central) - encouraged States to adopt; check your State.

Lease vs licence (key distinctions): (1) Interest: lease creates an interest in the property; licence is a personal privilege; (2) Transferability: lease is transferable; licence is not; (3) Revocability: lease is not revocable (except by determination in accordance with the Act); licence is revocable (subject to Easements Act Sec 60); (4) Heritability: lease passes to the legal representatives; licence terminates on the death of the licensor/ licensee; (5) Possession: lessee has exclusive possession; licensee has only the right of occupation; (6) Suing: lessee can sue trespassers; licensee cannot. Court looks at substance and not the label (Associated Hotels of India v R.N. Kapoor; B.M. Lall v Dunlop Rubber, 1968).

landmark_cases.principle: Waiver/ forfeiture and acceptance of rent.

common_traps: Sec 106: AGRICULTURAL/ MANUFACTURING = year to year + 6 months' notice; OTHERS = month to month + 15 days' notice.
Sec 107: lease > 1 year, year to year or yearly rent = REGISTERED instrument. Lease up to one year = registered or oral with possession.
Sec 117: Chapter on lease does not apply to agricultural leases unless notified.
Sec 111(g) forfeiture needs a written notice of intention to determine; waiver under Sec 112 by acceptance of rent.
Sec 116 - holding over requires lessor's acceptance of rent or assent; otherwise tenant is a tenant at sufferance.
