Lease for 1 year and above must be made by: registered instrument.
Effect of holding over: Sec 116.
Which of the following is a licence? ... Easements Act Sec 52.

sections.title: Exchange, Gift and Actionable Claims (Secs 118-137)
sections.summary: Gift (Secs 122-129) is the most-tested; exchange and actionable claims are short and bare-act based.
key_points: Sec 118 EXCHANGE: when two persons mutually transfer the ownership of one thing for the ownership of another, neither thing nor both things being money only, the transaction is called an exchange. A transfer of property in completion of an exchange can be made only in a manner provided for the transfer of such property by sale. Sec 119: right of party deprived of thing received in exchange - the party is entitled to compensation for loss from defective title. Sec 120: rights and liabilities of parties to an exchange are the same as those of a seller as to the thing he gives and of a buyer as to the thing he takes. Exchange of immovable property valued Rs 100 or more: registered instrument.

Sec 122 GIFT: the transfer of certain existing movable or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration, by one person, called the donor, to another, called the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Such acceptance must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while he is still capable of giving. If the donee dies before acceptance, the gift is void. Essentials: (1) donor; (2) donee; (3) subject-matter - existing property (movable or immovable); (4) voluntary and without consideration; (5) acceptance by the donee during the donor's life while capable of giving.

Sec 123 MODE: for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses. For the purpose of making a gift of movable property, the transfer may be effected either by a registered instrument signed as aforesaid or by delivery. Such delivery may be made in the same way as goods sold may be delivered. Registration is mandatory for gift of immovable property irrespective of the value (Registration Act Sec 17(1)(a)). A registered gift deed need not be accompanied by delivery of possession: Renikuntla Rajamma v K. Sarwanamma (2014) - possession is not necessary for validity of a registered gift; acceptance may be implied (e.g., by taking the deed or benefits).

Sec 124: a gift comprising both existing and future property is void as to the latter. Sec 125: a gift of a thing to two or more donees, of whom one does not accept it, is void as to the interest which he would have taken had he accepted. Sec 126: the donor and donee may agree that on the happening of any specified event which does not depend on the will of the donor a gift shall be suspended or revoked; but a gift which the parties agree shall be revocable wholly or in part, at the mere will of the donor, is void wholly or in part, as the case may be. A gift may also be revoked in any of the cases (save want or failure of consideration) in which, if it were a contract, it might be rescinded (e.g., fraud, undue influence, mistake). Sec 127: onerous gift - where a gift is in the form of a single transfer to the same person of several things of which one is, and the others are not, burdened by an obligation, the donee can take nothing by the gift unless he accepts it fully. Sec 128: universal donee - where a gift consists of the donor's whole property, the donee is personally liable for all the debts due and liabilities incurred by the donor at the time of the gift, to the extent of the property comprised in it. Sec 129: nothing in this chapter relates to gifts of movable property made in contemplation of death (donatio mortis causa), or shall be deemed to affect any rule of Muhammadan law (hiba) or Mohammedan law or of Hindu law (as saved) - Muslim gifts (hiba) need declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession and no registration (Mohammedan Law).

Gift vs Will: gift operates immediately (inter vivos) and is irrevocable (except Sec 126); a will operates after death and is revocable. Gift vs Sale: no consideration in gift. Gift to a minor: valid, accepted by guardian. Gift by a person of unsound mind or minor: void. Gift made by a pardanashin woman, the donee must prove it was an act of free will with independent advice.

ACTIONABLE CLAIMS - Sec 3: 'actionable claim' means a claim to any debt, other than a debt secured by the mortgage of immovable property or by hypothecation or pledge of movable property, or to any beneficial interest in movable property not in the possession, either actual or constructive, of the claimant, which the Civil Courts recognise as affording grounds for relief, whether such debt or beneficial interest be existent, accruing, conditional or contingent. Examples: book debts, arrears of rent, insurance policy claims, unsecured debts, a right to future dividends (as to arrears). Not actionable: claims secured by mortgage/ pledge; a claim to immovable property; a right to damages for tort (an unliquidated damages claim is a mere right to sue, not transferable); a claim not recognised by law (gambling debt).

Sec 130 TRANSFER: the transfer of an actionable claim shall be effected only by the execution of an instrument in writing signed by the transferor or his duly authorised agent, shall be complete and effectual upon the execution of such instrument, and thereupon all the rights and remedies of the transferor, whether by way of damages or otherwise, shall vest in the transferee, whether such notice of the transfer as is hereinafter provided be given or not (provided that every dealing with the debt or other actionable claim by the debtor or other person from whom the transferor would, but for such instrument of transfer as aforesaid, have been entitled to receive or enforce such debt or other actionable claim, bona fide and before he has notice of the transfer shall be valid). The transferee may sue in his own name (no need for the transferor to be joined). The transfer must be in writing; an endorsement on a deed/ instrument is not enough unless it is a transfer in writing signed by the transferor; no registration is needed (it's a movable property, though documentary evidence may need stamp duty). Sec 131: notice of transfer must be in writing signed by the transferor or his agent (or, if refused, by the transferee) stating the name and address of the transferee; Sec 132: liability of transferee of actionable claim - the transferee takes subject to all the liabilities and equities to which the transferor was subject in respect thereof at the date of the transfer. Sec 133: warranty of solvency of debtor - in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the transferor of a debt warrants the existence of the debt at the time of the transfer, but not the solvency of the debtor. Sec 134-136: mortgaged debt transferred; Sec 136: incapacity of officers connected with courts of justice (judges, pleaders, officers) - they cannot buy actionable claims falling within the jurisdiction of their court; such transfers are void. Sec 137: saving of negotiable instruments, and of the provisions of Sec 6/ of the Companies Act.

landmark_cases.case: Renikuntla Rajamma v K. Sarwanamma (2014)
landmark_cases.principle: A registered gift deed is valid even without delivery of possession; acceptance may be inferred.

landmark_cases.case: Asokan v Lakshmikutty (2007)
landmark_cases.principle: Acceptance of gift, possession and its relevance (gifts under TPA).

common_traps: Gift of IMMOVABLE property: registered instrument, signed by donor, attested by at least 2 witnesses - ALWAYS (no value threshold).
Gift of movable property: registered instrument OR delivery.
Gift of future property is void to that extent (Sec 124). A gift revocable at the donor's mere will is void.
Actionable claim: transfer is complete on execution of an instrument in writing; notice to the debtor is NOT a condition of validity (only protects the debtor).
Muslim gifts are outside Chapter VII (Sec 129).
likely_questions: Gift is defined in: Sec 122.
Gift of immovable property requires: registered instrument attested by 2 witnesses.
Actionable claim is transferred by: instrument in writing signed by the transferor.
Universal donee: Sec 128 - liable for debts to the extent of the property gifted.

sections.title: Easements and Licences (Indian Easements Act 1882)
sections.summary: Definition (Sec 4), kinds, acquisition by prescription (Sec 15), extinction and licence (Secs 52-63).
key_points: Sec 4: an easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own. Dominant heritage = land for whose beneficial enjoyment the right exists; dominant owner = owner of dominant heritage; servient heritage and owner = land on which the liability is imposed. Easement is an incorporeal right attached to land; it is not a personal right; it cannot exist apart from the dominant heritage (Sec 6(c) TPA).

Characteristics: (1) imposed by dominant on servient heritage; (2) the right must be for the beneficial enjoyment of the dominant heritage; (3) the two heritages must be owned by different persons; (4) it is a right without profit (no right to take anything - profit a prendre is a different right); (5) it is a right of 'user' not 'possession'. Examples: right of way, right to light and air, right to the flow of water, right of support, right of drainage.

Kinds: continuous (enjoyment without act of man - e.g., light and air) and discontinuous (needs an act of man - right of way); apparent (visible sign) and non-apparent; positive (the right to do something) and negative (prevent something). Also easements of necessity, quasi-easements, customary easements, and acquired by prescription.

ACQUISITION: by grant (express or implied - Sec 8), by necessity (Sec 13) and quasi-easements, by prescription (Sec 15), by custom (Sec 18), and by transfer. Sec 15 PRESCRIPTION: where the access and use of light or air to and for any building have been peaceably enjoyed therewith as an easement, and as of right, without interruption, and for twenty years, and where support from one person's land or things affixed thereto has been peaceably received by another person's land subjected to or things affixed thereto as an easement, and as of right, without interruption, for twenty years, and where a right of way or any other easement has been peaceably and openly enjoyed by any person claiming title thereto, as an easement, and as of right, without interruption, and for twenty years, the right to such access and use of light or air, support, or other easement, shall be absolute. Each of the said periods of twenty years shall be taken to be a period ending within two years next before the institution of the suit wherein the claim to which such period relates is contested. Where the property over which a right is claimed belongs to Government, the period is thirty years. Enjoyment must be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario (without force, secrecy or permission).

Sec 13: easements of necessity (a person transferring or bequeathing immovable property is entitled to a way of necessity); Sec 14: quasi-easements arising on a severance of tenements; Sec 16: exclusion of days of disability; Sec 12: who may impose easements (owner of the heritage); Sec 17: easements acquired by a person with no title; Secs 24-25: exercise of an easement - the extent of user must not be altered; Sec 32: no liability for interruption. Extinction (Secs 37-47): by dissolution of right of servient owner; by expiry of limited period; by release; by revocation; by unity of ownership (merger - Sec 45 related); by permanent change in the dominant heritage; by necessity ceasing; by non-user for twenty years (Sec 46: easement of necessity extinguished when necessity ends); and abandonment.

Sec 52 LICENCE: where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a licence. Sec 53: who may grant; Sec 54: licence may be express or implied; Sec 56: licence is not transferable, and not assignable; Sec 60: A licence may be revoked by the grantor, unless (a) it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force; (b) the licensee, acting upon the licence, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution. Sec 62: a licence is deemed to be revoked (a) when, from a cause preceding the grant of it, the grantor ceases to have any interest in the property affected by the licence; (b) when the licensee dies or ceases to occupy the property; (c) when the licensee becomes insolvent; (d) when the licence is granted for a term and the term expires; (e) in case of licence for a particular purpose, when the purpose is attained or abandoned; (f) when the licensee assigns the licence. Sec 63: where a licence is revoked, the licensee is entitled to a reasonable time to leave the property and remove his goods. Sec 64: licensee's right to compensation if revoked wrongly.

Remedies: suit for injunction/ damages (Sec 33 Easements Act: suit for compensation for obstruction of easement); the Specific Relief Act Secs 38-42 apply. Easement by prescription cannot be acquired against a co-owner's property by a co-owner, and a tenant can acquire an easement for his landlord's benefit only.
common_traps: Easement vs licence: easement is an interest; licence is a personal permission, revocable unless Sec 60 exceptions.
Prescription: 20 years (private land); 30 years (Government land).
Easement cannot be separated from the dominant heritage; it is not transferable apart from it.
likely_questions: Period for acquiring easement by prescription: 20 years (30 years against Government).
Licence is defined in Sec 52 of the Easements Act.
A licence coupled with a transfer of property: irrevocable (Sec 60(a)).

sections.title: Registration Act 1908 (essentials for property questions)
sections.summary: Sec 17 (compulsory registration), Secs 23-25 (time), Sec 47 (relation back), Sec 49 (effect of non-registration) are frequent AIBE targets.
key_points: Sec 17(1) COMPULSORILY REGISTRABLE documents (if relating to immovable property): (a) instruments of gift of immovable property; (b) other non-testamentary instruments which purport or operate to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish, whether in present or in future, any right, title or interest, whether vested or contingent, of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, to or in immovable property; (c) non-testamentary instruments which acknowledge the receipt or payment of any consideration on account of the creation, declaration, assignment, limitation or extinction of any such right, title or interest; (d) leases of immovable property from year to year, or for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent; (e) non-testamentary instruments transferring or assigning any decree or order of a court or any award when such decree or order or award purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish, whether in present or in future, any right, title or interest, whether vested or contingent, of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, to or in immovable property. Sec 17(1A) (inserted 2001): documents containing contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property for the purpose of Sec 53A of the TPA must be registered if they have been executed on or after the commencement of the Registration and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Act 2001; otherwise they shall have no effect for the purposes of Sec 53A.

Sec 17(2) EXCEPTIONS (documents that need not be registered even if they relate to immovable property): composition deeds; instruments relating to shares in a joint stock company not creating rights in immovable property; debentures and their endorsement/transfer; documents merely creating a right to obtain another document (but see Sec 17(1A)); receipts for consideration and assignments of money decrees; Government grants; partition instruments made by a Revenue Officer; certain loan orders under the Land Improvement Loans Act and Agriculturists' Loans Act; and certificates of sale granted to purchasers at public auction by a Civil or Revenue Officer. Wills are optionally registrable (Sec 18(e)); an unregistered will is valid.

Sec 18: optional registration (e.g., wills, instruments not requiring registration under Sec 17, instruments relating to movable property). Sec 23: TIME for presentation - a document (other than a will) must be presented for registration within FOUR MONTHS from the date of its execution; if the document is a decree or order, within 4 months from the day on which the decree or order was made (or becomes final in appeal). Sec 24: documents executed by several persons at different times - within 4 months of each execution. Sec 25: delay - where, owing to urgent necessity or unavoidable accident, a document is not presented within the time, the Registrar may, in cases where the delay in presentation does not exceed four months, direct that, on payment of a fine not exceeding ten times the amount of the proper registration-fee, such document shall be accepted for registration. Sec 32: persons who may present (the executant, claimant, or their agents/representatives). Sec 34: enquiry before registration (admission of execution; identity). Sec 35: procedure on admission and denial of execution. Sec 40: wills - may be presented by the testator or, after his death, by any person claiming as executor or otherwise under the will.

Sec 47: a registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration (relation back to date of execution). Sec 48: registered documents relating to property, when duly registered, take effect against oral agreements or declarations (unless accompanied by delivery of possession and Sec 53A applicable, Sec 48 - the 'exception' for oral agreements accompanied by delivery of possession which constitute a valid transfer under law). Sec 49: EFFECT OF NON-REGISTRATION: no document required by Sec 17 or by any provision of the TPA to be registered shall (a) affect any immovable property comprised therein, or (b) confer any power to adopt, or (c) be received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property or conferring such power, unless it has been registered. Proviso: an unregistered document affecting immovable property and required by this Act or the TPA to be registered may be received as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance or as evidence of part performance of a contract for the purposes of Sec 53A of the TPA, or as evidence of any collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument. (K.B. Saha & Sons v Development Consultant Ltd (2008): collateral-purpose principle). Sec 50: registered document relating to property has priority over unregistered ones.

Registration is constructive notice of the contents (Explanation 1 to Sec 3 TPA). A document registered in an office not having jurisdiction is still valid if registered by an office within the district. Registration does not validate a void document (it merely gives notice and satisfies the formal requirement). The Registrar can refuse registration on prescribed grounds (Sec 71 etc. - in the discharge of ministerial functions; the Registrar cannot adjudicate on title - Park View Enterprises v State of Tamil Nadu, 1990 - quasi-judicial functions not available).

Recent trend: online registration and e-stamping (State portals), Aadhaar-based identification, 'digital' presentation; the Registration Act being re-considered in the Draft Registration Bill 2013, not yet enacted. Real estate: RERA requires registered agreements for sale (Sec 13 RERA).

landmark_cases.case: K.B. Saha & Sons v Development Consultant Ltd (2008)
landmark_cases.principle: Unregistered documents can be used for collateral purposes (e.g., to prove the character of possession), not to prove the transaction itself.

landmark_cases.case: Suraj Lamp & Industries v State of Haryana (2012)
landmark_cases.principle: Only registered conveyance can transfer title to immovable property.

landmark_cases.case: Park View Enterprises v State of Tamil Nadu (1990)
landmark_cases.principle: Registering authority cannot decide the validity of title.

common_traps: Gift of immovable property: registration is compulsory REGARDLESS of value; sale/ mortgage/ lease - value threshold Rs 100 (lease: 1 year).
Time for presentation: 4 months from execution; further 4 months with fine up to ten times the registration fee (so the maximum is 8 months).
A registered document operates from the date of EXECUTION, not registration (Sec 47).
Wills: registration optional.
likely_questions: Time limit for presenting a document for registration: 4 months (Sec 23).
Fine for delay under Sec 25: up to ten times the registration fee.
Effect of non-registration: Sec 49.
Registered document operates from: date of execution (Sec 47).

sections.title: Negotiable Instruments: Definitions, Types and Parties (Secs 1-17)
sections.summary: Definitions of promissory note, bill of exchange, cheque; negotiability; holder vs holder in due course. Expect 1 conceptual question alongside the Sec 138 question.
key_points: Sec 13: a negotiable instrument means a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer. Characteristics: free transferability by delivery (bearer) or endorsement and delivery (order); the holder in due course gets good title free from defects of the transferor's title; the holder can sue in his own name; presumptions apply (Sec 118). Statutory negotiable instruments: only these three; others (hundis, bank drafts, dividend warrants, share warrants, railway receipts, bills of lading) are negotiable by custom or are not negotiable (documents of title).

Sec 4 PROMISSORY NOTE: an instrument in writing (not being a bank-note or a currency-note) containing an unconditional undertaking, signed by the maker, to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person, or to the bearer of the instrument. Essentials: in writing; promise to pay (not mere acknowledgment - 'I.O.U. Rs 500' is not a note); unconditional; signed by maker; certain parties; certain sum; payable in money only; stamped. A note payable to bearer on demand cannot be issued (Sec 31 RBI Act - only RBI/Government can issue bearer demand notes).

Sec 5 BILL OF EXCHANGE: an instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument. Three parties: drawer (maker), drawee (the person directed to pay), payee. The drawee becomes ACCEPTOR on accepting the bill by signing. Sec 7: drawer, drawee, drawee in case of need, acceptor, acceptor for honour, payee. Sec 6 CHEQUE: a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand, and it includes the electronic image of a truncated cheque and a cheque in the electronic form (Explanation I - added in 2002). Cheque = a bill of exchange drawn on a banker, payable on demand. A cheque does not require acceptance and has no days of grace. Cheque validity: three months from the date of drawing (RBI Circular, effective 1 April 2012).

Sec 8: HOLDER - the person entitled in his own name to the possession of the instrument and to receive or recover the amount due thereon from the parties thereto. A mere custodian (agent) is not a holder. Sec 9 HOLDER IN DUE COURSE (HDC): any person who for consideration became the possessor of a promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque if payable to bearer, or the payee or indorsee thereof, if payable to order, before the amount mentioned in it became payable, and without having sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived his title. Essentials: (1) for consideration; (2) became possessor before maturity; (3) in good faith, without notice of defect; (4) payee or endorsee/ bearer. Privileges: (Sec 53) good title; free from defects of the previous holder's title (fraud, no consideration) and defences available against prior parties; (Sec 118) presumption of HDC status (but see Sec 58 - if obtained by fraud/ unlawful means, the burden of proof is on the holder). A payee can be HDC (Sec 9), though for some purposes the payee cannot be a holder in due course against the drawer in a defence of lack of consideration between those two.

Sec 10: PAYMENT IN DUE COURSE - payment in accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument, in good faith and without negligence, to any person in possession thereof under circumstances which do not afford a reasonable ground for believing that he is not entitled to receive payment of the amount therein mentioned. Sec 14: NEGOTIATION - when a promissory note, bill or cheque is transferred to any person so as to constitute that person the holder thereof, the instrument is said to be negotiated. Sec 15: ENDORSEMENT - when the maker or holder of a negotiable instrument signs the same, otherwise than as such maker, for the purpose of negotiating the same, on the back or face thereof, or on a slip of paper annexed thereto, or so signs for the same purpose a stamped paper intended to be completed as a negotiable instrument, he is said to endorse the same, and is called the endorser. Sec 16: endorsement in blank vs in full - if the endorser signs his name only, the endorsement is in blank (instrument becomes payable to bearer); if he adds a direction to pay to a specified person, it is in full. Sec 17: effect of endorsement - the endorsement of a negotiable instrument followed by delivery transfers to the endorsee the property therein with the right of further negotiation; but the endorsement may, by express words, restrict or exclude such right (restrictive endorsement: 'pay A only'; 'sans recours'; conditional endorsement).

Sec 18-20: ambiguous instruments - holder may treat as either promissory note or bill; Sec 20: INCHOATE STAMPED INSTRUMENTS - where one person signs and delivers to another a paper stamped in accordance with the law relating to negotiable instruments then in force in India, and either wholly blank or having written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument, he thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete, as the case may be, upon it a negotiable instrument, for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp. The person so signing shall be liable upon such instrument, in the capacity in which he signed the same, to any holder in due course for such amount. (Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar, 2019: even a blank signed cheque voluntarily handed over attracts presumption under Sec 139.)

Sec 21-25: At sight / on demand / after sight; Sec 22 MATURITY - the maturity of a promissory note or bill of exchange is the date at which it falls due. Every promissory note or bill of exchange which is not expressed to be payable on demand, at sight or on presentment is at maturity on the third day after the day on which it is expressed to be payable (three days of grace). Sec 23: calculating maturity of bill or note payable so many months after date or sight; Sec 24: so many days after date or sight (the day of presentation/date excluded); Sec 25: when the day of maturity is a public holiday, the instrument shall be deemed due on the NEXT PRECEDING BUSINESS DAY (this is the opposite of the Contract Act/ General Clauses Act approach).

Sec 26-30: capacity - every person capable of contracting can bind himself and be bound by making, drawing, acceptance, endorsement, delivery and negotiation; a minor may draw, endorse, deliver and negotiate so as to bind all parties except himself (Sec 26). Sec 27: agency - may sign through an agent; Sec 28: liability of agent signing - where the agent signs in his own name, he is personally liable unless he indicates that he is signing as agent (Sec 28: an agent who signs his name 'without indicating that he is signing as agent' is personally liable; Sec 27 for the principal). Sec 29: liability of legal representative. Sec 30: LIABILITY OF DRAWER - the drawer of a bill of exchange or cheque is bound, in case of dishonour by the drawee or acceptor thereof, to compensate the holder, provided due notice of dishonour has been given to, or received by, the drawer. Sec 31: LIABILITY OF DRAWEE OF CHEQUE - the drawee of a cheque having sufficient funds of the drawer in his hands properly applicable to the payment of such cheque must pay the cheque when duly required so to do, and, in default of such payment, must compensate the drawer for any loss or damage caused by such default. Sec 32: liability of maker of note and acceptor of bill - in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the maker of a promissory note and the acceptor before maturity of a bill of exchange are bound to pay the amount thereof at maturity according to the apparent tenor of the note or acceptance respectively (principal debtors). Sec 35: liability of endorser - in the absence of a contract to the contrary, whoever endorses and delivers a negotiable instrument before maturity, without in such endorsement expressly excluding or making conditional his own liability, is bound thereby to every subsequent holder, in case of dishonour by the drawee, acceptor or maker, to compensate such holder for any loss or damage caused to him by such dishonour, provided due notice of dishonour has been given. Sec 37: maker, drawer and acceptor principals; the others sureties. Sec 43: a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, endorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails, creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction (but if any such party has transferred the instrument with or without endorsement to a holder for consideration, such holder, and every subsequent holder deriving title from him, may recover the amount due on such instrument from the transferor for consideration or any prior party thereto). Sec 44: partial failure of consideration. Sec 46-48: delivery; negotiation by delivery (bearer instruments) and by endorsement and delivery (order instruments).

DISHONOUR (Secs 91-98): dishonour by non-acceptance (Sec 91) and dishonour by non-payment (Sec 92); Sec 93: notice of dishonour must be given by the holder to all prior parties who he wishes to make liable; Sec 94: mode; Sec 98: when notice of dishonour is unnecessary (e.g., when the party charged has dispensed with notice, when the drawer has countermanded payment, the drawer could not suffer damage from the want of notice); Secs 99-104: noting and protest (protest: foreign bills; protest is a formal certificate by a notary public). Sec 82: discharge of parties from liability - by cancellation, release, payment; Sec 87: MATERIAL ALTERATION - any material alteration of a negotiable instrument renders the same void as against any one who is a party thereto at the time of making such alteration and does not consent thereto, unless it was made in order to carry out the common intention of the original parties. Alterations that are material: date, sum payable, time of payment, place of payment, rate of interest, addition of a party, crossing, striking out words; (Sec 89: payment in due course of altered cheque - the banker is protected if the alteration was not apparent). In the 2026 Supreme Court ruling (decided 17 July 2026), conviction under Sec 138 was set aside where the cheque bore visible tampering - the Court held no extra proof was needed where the alteration was patent.

CROSSING OF CHEQUES (Secs 123-131A): Sec 123 - general crossing: the cheque bears across its face an addition of the words 'and company' or any abbreviation thereof, between two parallel transverse lines, or two parallel transverse lines simply, either with or without the words 'not negotiable' - the banker shall not pay it otherwise than to a banker. Sec 124 - special crossing: the name of a banker is added across its face - payable only to that banker. Sec 125: crossing after issue - the holder may cross a cheque generally or specially, and add 'not negotiable'; Sec 126: payment of crossed cheque; Sec 129: protection of banker; Sec 130: cheque bearing 'not negotiable' - the transferee of such a cheque cannot have, and cannot give, a better title than the transferor had (it remains negotiable/ transferable, but loses its characteristic of conferring better title); Sec 131: non-liability of banker receiving payment of crossed cheque (COLLECTING BANKER) - a banker who has in good faith and without negligence received payment for a customer of a cheque crossed generally or specially to himself shall not, in case the title to the cheque proves defective, incur any liability to the true owner of the cheque by reason only of having received such payment. Sec 131A: the provisions apply to drafts.

PRESUMPTIONS (Sec 118): until the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed (a) of consideration - that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; (b) as to date - that every negotiable instrument bearing a date was made or drawn on such date; (c) as to time of acceptance; (d) as to time of transfer; (e) as to order of endorsements; (f) as to stamps - that a lost promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque was duly stamped; (g) that the holder of a negotiable instrument is a holder in due course (except in the case of Sec 58). Sec 119: Sec 119 - presumption on proof of protest; Sec 120: estoppel against denying the original validity of the instrument - no maker of a promissory note, and no drawer of a bill of exchange or cheque, and no acceptor of a bill for the honour of the drawer shall, in a suit thereon by a holder in due course, be permitted to deny the validity of the instrument as originally made or drawn; Sec 121: estoppel against denying capacity of payee to endorse; Sec 122: estoppel against denying signature or capacity of prior party.
common_traps: Cheque is payable ON DEMAND only; days of grace do not apply to cheques/ demand instruments.
Holder in due course must have taken BEFORE maturity and for CONSIDERATION and in good faith.
Sec 25: if the maturity day is a public holiday, due on the preceding business day.
Crossing 'not negotiable' does not make the cheque non-transferable; it only removes the ability to confer better title (Sec 130).
Under Sec 6, electronic image of truncated cheque (CTS) and cheque in electronic form are cheques.
Sec 118 presumptions are rebuttable.

sections.title: Dishonour of Cheque: Section 138 (Chapter XVII, Secs 138-148)
sections.summary: The most predictable AIBE area within Part 7. Statutory timelines, presumptions, jurisdiction (Sec 142(2)), interim compensation (Sec 143A), appellate deposit (Sec 148), compounding (Sec 147). 2025-26 Supreme Court decisions have been numerous; the principles behind them are fair game.
key_points: BACKGROUND: Chapter XVII (Secs 138-142) was inserted by the Banking, Public Financial Institutions and Negotiable Instruments Laws (Amendment) Act 1988 to promote the credibility of cheques. Amendments: 2002 (Secs 143-147 added; summary trial; 30-day notice; 15-day payment period), 2015 (Sec 142(2) and 142A - territorial jurisdiction), 2018 (Sec 143A interim compensation; Sec 148 deposit in appeal; maximum punishment raised from 1 year to 2 years). Criminal liability for cheque dishonour is a civil wrong made criminal; but the offence is compoundable (Sec 147).

SEC 138 - ESSENTIALS: (1) a cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker; (2) for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account; (3) for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability (Explanation: legally enforceable debt or other liability); (4) the cheque is returned by the bank unpaid either because the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque, or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank; (5) the cheque was presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it was drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier (practically THREE MONTHS since RBI's circular of 1 April 2012); (6) the payee or holder in due course makes a DEMAND for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a NOTICE in writing to the drawer within THIRTY DAYS of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; (7) the drawer fails to make payment within FIFTEEN DAYS of the receipt of the said notice. If these ingredients are satisfied, the drawer is deemed to have committed an offence, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to TWO YEARS, or with fine which may extend to TWICE the amount of the cheque, or with both.

Dishonour for reasons other than insufficiency of funds - 'payment stopped by drawer', 'account closed', 'refer to drawer', 'signature differs/ not as per specimen' etc. Courts have held that stop-payment instructions and account closure attract Sec 138 (the Sec 138 purpose of preventing dishonour; Modi Cements v Kuchil Kumar Nandi, 1998; Goa Plast v Chico Ursula D'Souza, 2004). However, a cheque with a patent material alteration cannot found a conviction (SC, 17 July 2026).

NOTICE: the notice must be in writing, must demand the cheque amount (not a larger sum - Suman Sethi v Ajay K. Churiwal, 2000 - a notice demanding a sum with other claims was held vitiated only if the cheque amount isn't separately demanded), and must be given within 30 days of receipt of the bank's information. A notice sent to the correct address by registered post is presumed served (Sec 27 General Clauses Act; C.C. Alavi Haji v Palapetty Muhammed, 2007 - the drawer cannot defeat the complaint by saying he did not receive the notice; he must pay within 15 days of the deemed receipt). Notice can also be given by email/ other electronic modes (Information Technology Act); a notice by the payee's authorised agent/ advocate is valid.

CAUSE OF ACTION AND LIMITATION (Sec 142): a court takes cognizance only on a written complaint made by the payee or holder in due course, within ONE MONTH of the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Sec 138 (i.e., from the expiry of the 15 days). The Court may take cognizance after the prescribed period if the complainant satisfies it that he had sufficient cause for not making a complaint within such period (Sec 142(1)(b)); the SC (2026 quarterly digest) addressed the sequencing of condonation of delay and cognizance. No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class shall try an offence under Sec 138. Complaint can be filed by an authorised representative; a company (as complainant) acts through an authorised person. Cheque may be presented multiple times within its validity period, but only ONE cause of action arises from the notice following the dishonour on a presentation (MSR Leathers v S. Palaniappan, 2013: successive presentations are allowed; failure to file complaint after the first dishonour does not bar a complaint after the later one). In January 2026, the Supreme Court held that dishonour of multiple cheques issued in the same transaction can give rise to separate causes of action and separate complaints.

SEC 142(2) TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION (as inserted in 2015, with Sec 142A): the offence under Sec 138 shall be inquired into and tried only by a court within whose local jurisdiction, (a) if the cheque is delivered for collection through an account, the branch of the bank where the payee or holder in due course, as the case may be, maintains the account, is situated; or (b) if the cheque is presented for payment otherwise than through an account, the branch of the drawee bank where the drawer maintains the account, is situated. Explanation: where a cheque is delivered for collection at any branch of the bank of the payee or holder in due course, then, the cheque shall be deemed to have been delivered to the branch of the bank in which the payee or holder in due course, as the case may be, maintains the account. This overrides Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v State of Maharashtra (2014), which had held that the place of the drawee bank was the place of jurisdiction. Sec 142A validated the transfer of pending cases. Bridgestone India v Inderpal Singh (2016) clarified the 2015 Amendment's retrospectivity.

SEC 139 PRESUMPTION IN FAVOUR OF THE HOLDER: it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Sec 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Sec 139 presumption includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt (Rangappa v Sri Mohan, 2010). The presumption is rebuttable; the accused need not step into the witness box and may rely on the material on record; the standard is 'preponderance of probabilities' (not beyond reasonable doubt - Basalingappa v Mudibasappa, 2019; Kumar Exports v Sharma Carpets, 2009). A signed blank cheque voluntarily handed over attracts the presumption (Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar, 2019). In August 2026 the Supreme Court restated that a mere denial of debt or consideration is not enough to rebut the presumption. In April 2026 (Renuka v State of Maharashtra) the Court held that where the basic ingredients of Sec 138 are made out, the complaint cannot be quashed at the pre-trial stage on the ground that the cheque was not issued for a debt - that is a matter of trial. The Court has also held that a time-barred debt may still be a 'legally enforceable debt' only if the cheque amounts to a fresh promise within Sec 25(3) of the Contract Act (check the cases before relying), and that violation of Sec 269SS of the Income-tax Act (cash loan above the prescribed limit) does not automatically make the debt unenforceable (discussed in Sanjabij Tari v Kishore S. Borcar - verify the exact holding before citing in an examination of case law).

SEC 140: it shall not be a defence in a prosecution for an offence under Sec 138 that the drawer had no reason to believe when he issued the cheque that the cheque may be dishonoured on presentment for the reasons stated in that section. SEC 141 OFFENCES BY COMPANIES: where an offence under Sec 138 has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty and shall be liable to be proceeded against. Proviso: not liable if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge, or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent it. Sec 141(2): where the offence is committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to the neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such person shall also be deemed guilty. Principles: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals v Neeta Bhalla (2005) - the complaint must specifically aver that the director was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business; mere designation as director is not enough; but a signatory to the cheque is liable by virtue of signing; Aneeta Hada v Godfather Travels (2012) - the company must be arraigned as an accused for the directors to be prosecuted (the company is the principal offender); Pooja Ravinder Devidasani v State of Maharashtra (2014) - non-executive directors and those who resigned cannot be roped in without specific allegations. Also: the partnership firm is a 'company' for Sec 141 (Explanation: 'company' means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals; 'director' in relation to a firm means a partner).

SEC 143 SUMMARY TRIAL: notwithstanding anything in the CrPC (read now with the BNSS 2023), all offences under Sec 138 shall be tried by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class or by a Metropolitan Magistrate, and the provisions of Secs 262 to 265 (both inclusive) of the CrPC shall, as far as may be, apply to such trials (now the summary trial provisions of Secs 283-288 BNSS, saved/ applied through the General Clauses Act and Sec 531 BNSS). In the case of conviction in a summary trial, it shall be lawful for the Magistrate to pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding ONE YEAR and an amount of fine exceeding five thousand rupees. If, at the commencement of or in the course of a summary trial, it appears that a sentence of imprisonment exceeding one year may have to be passed, the Magistrate shall after hearing the parties record an order to that effect and thereafter recall any witness who may have been examined and proceed to hear or rehear the case in the manner provided by the Code (conversion to summons case). Sec 143(3): the trial shall be conducted as expeditiously as possible and an endeavour shall be made to conclude the trial within six months from the date of filing of the complaint. Meters and Instruments v Kanchan Mehta (2018): guidelines on summary trial, compounding, and conversion.

SEC 143A INTERIM COMPENSATION (2018): (1) notwithstanding anything contained in the CrPC, the Court trying an offence under Sec 138 may order the drawer of the cheque to pay interim compensation to the complainant (a) in a summary trial or a summons case, where he pleads not guilty to the accusation made in the complaint; and (b) in any other case, upon framing of charge. (2) The interim compensation shall not exceed TWENTY PER CENT of the amount of the cheque. (3) It shall be paid within SIXTY DAYS from the date of the order, or within such further period not exceeding THIRTY DAYS as may be directed by the Court on sufficient cause being shown. (4) If the drawer is acquitted, the Court shall direct the complainant to repay to the drawer the amount so paid with interest at the bank rate as published by the RBI, prevailing at the beginning of the relevant financial year, within 60 days (extendable by 30 days). The recovery may be made as if it were a fine under Sec 421 CrPC (now under the BNSS). The provision is directory/ 'may' (Rakesh Ranjan Srivastava v State of Jharkhand, 2023) but, per G.J. Raja v Tejraj Surana (2019), Sec 143A applies only to offences committed after 1 September 2018 (it is prospective). The complainant who is a 'victim' can appeal (Sec 372 CrPC proviso/ Sec 413 BNSS).

SEC 144: mode of service of summons - by speed post/ approved courier; Sec 145: evidence on affidavit - the evidence of the complainant may be given by him on affidavit and may, subject to all just exceptions, be read in evidence in any enquiry, trial or other proceeding; the Court may, if it thinks fit, and shall, on the application of the prosecution or the accused, summon and examine any person giving evidence on affidavit as to the facts contained therein. Sec 146: banks' slip or memo having thereon the official mark denoting that the cheque has been dishonoured shall be prima facie evidence of the fact of dishonour (court shall presume the genuineness of such mark unless disproved). Sec 147: OFFENCES TO BE COMPOUNDABLE - notwithstanding anything contained in the CrPC, every offence punishable under this Act shall be compoundable. Damodar S. Prabhu v Sayed Babalal H (2010): guidelines to encourage compounding by costs payable to the Legal Services Authority at the rate of: no costs if compounded at the first or second hearing; 10% of the cheque amount (before Magistrate at later stage); 15% (Sessions Court/ High Court); 20% (Supreme Court). The recent decision in Sanjabij Tari v Kishore S. Borcar consolidated the procedural directions in NI Act cases and modified the compounding framework - read the latest cost schedule in the judgment before relying on figures.

SEC 148 DEPOSIT IN APPEAL (2018): in an appeal by the drawer against conviction under Sec 138, the Appellate Court may order the appellant to deposit such sum which shall be a minimum of TWENTY PER CENT of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial court. This amount is in addition to any interim compensation paid under Sec 143A. It shall be deposited within 60 days (extendable by 30 days). The Appellate Court may direct release of the amount to the complainant at any time during the pendency of the appeal. Surinder Singh Deswal v Virender Gandhi (2019): Sec 148 applies to appeals even in cases for cheque offences committed before the 2018 Amendment (appeals filed after 1 September 2018); the word 'may' is to be read as 'shall' normally - the 20% deposit should ordinarily be directed except for special reasons (Jamboo Bhandari v M.P. State Industrial Development Corp, 2023).

OTHER LEADING DEVELOPMENTS: (a) Indian Bank Association v Union of India (2014) - directions for speedy disposal; (b) In Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under Section 138 of NI Act (2021) - Suo Motu; special courts and guidelines (including online summons); (c) Sripati Singh v State of Jharkhand (2021) - security cheques: if the debt is crystallised/ due, a cheque given as security may attract Sec 138; (d) P. Mohanraj v Shah Brothers Ispat (2021) - the moratorium under Sec 14 of the IBC bars Sec 138 proceedings against the corporate debtor, but not against its directors/ signatories (natural persons); the individual-insolvency moratorium (Sec 96, Part III IBC) and its effect on Sec 138 was considered by the Supreme Court in a 2026 ruling - read the judgment for the exact outcome; (e) 4 November 2026 - the Supreme Court held that an Asset Reconstruction Company that takes over a debt (assignee of the loan) can step into the shoes of the bank and pursue a Sec 138 prosecution on the dishonoured cheque (the cheque 'travels with the loan'); (f) 16 April 2026 (Canara Bank v Kavita Chowdhary) - a bank's failure to present a cheque within its validity period as agent for its customer can amount to deficiency in service under the Consumer Protection Act; (g) The legislature has repeatedly considered decriminalisation of Sec 138; as of now it remains a criminal offence (the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 did not decriminalise Sec 138).

ADMINISTRATIVE POINTS for exam: (i) 'Drawer' liable; payee/ holder in due course complains; (ii) the offence is a 'non-cognizable' offence/ summons case; (iii) A person cannot be convicted under Sec 138 for an unsigned cheque; (iv) The cheque must relate to a legally enforceable debt existing on the date of the cheque; a post-dated cheque is a cheque only on its date - presenting before the date is premature (Sec 138 offence is not committed if the cheque is dishonoured before the date); (v) 'Account payee' cheques have no effect on Sec 138; (vi) The offence is personal to the drawer; legal heirs are not criminally liable, though civil liability may continue.

modules.title: Land Acquisition (RFCTLARR Act 2013; Land Acquisition Act 1894 background)

sections.title: Constitutional Framework and Evolution
sections.summary: Background questions: Art 300A, eminent domain, the shift from the 1894 Act to the 2013 Act. Recent 7-judge Bench ruling on Art 300A is a hot topic.
key_points: Eminent domain = the sovereign power of the State to take private property for public purpose upon payment of compensation. Original Constitution: Art 31 (right to property as a Fundamental Right) with compensation; Art 19(1)(f) right to acquire, hold and dispose of property. The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) deleted Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 and inserted ARTICLE 300A in Part XII (Chapter IV): 'No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.' Right to property is now a constitutional right (not a fundamental right) and a statutory/ legal right (Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v State of Gujarat, 1994; Vidya Devi v State of Himachal Pradesh, 2020 - right to property is also a human right; the State cannot claim title by adverse possession against a citizen it has dispossessed without following due process of law).

Entry 42, List III (Concurrent List): 'Acquisition and requisitioning of property' - both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate. Hence State amendments to the 2013 Act (with Presidential assent under Art 254(2)) in several States.

The Land Acquisition Act 1894 (colonial) - broad powers; low compensation; no R&R; 'urgency clause' misuse. It was amended in 1984. The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 (RFCTLARR Act or 'LARR Act') - enacted on 26 September 2013 and brought into force on 1 January 2014; it repealed the 1894 Act (Sec 114) subject to savings. The 2015 Ordinances (to dilute consent and SIA requirements) lapsed; a Bill to the same effect lapsed in 2015. Several States (e.g., Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) enacted State amendments to exempt particular projects from consent/ SIA requirements.

Kolkata Municipal Corporation v Bimal Kumar Shaw (SC, 8 January 2024, 7-judge Bench): right to property under Art 300A is more than a bare right; the State's power to deprive a person of property must follow a procedure encompassing seven sub-rights: (i) the right to notice; (ii) the right to be heard (objections); (iii) the right to a reasoned decision; (iv) the duty to acquire only for public purpose; (v) the right of restitution or fair compensation; (vi) the right to an efficient and expeditious process; (vii) the right of conclusion (the final conclusion of the proceeding). Non-compliance can vitiate the deprivation. Expect a direct question on this.

K.T. Plantation v State of Karnataka (2011): Art 300A requires a law, public purpose is implicit, and compensation is not necessarily a requirement of the Article but arbitrary or illusory compensation can be challenged; Tarsem Singh (2019) and others emphasise that fair compensation is a statutory entitlement. State of Haryana v Mukesh Kumar (2011): right to property is a human right.

sections.title: The Land Acquisition Act 1894 (what still matters)
sections.summary: Because pending cases and Sec 24 of the 2013 Act refer to 1894 Act sections, AIBE may ask one or two section-level questions. Memorise the process chain.
key_points: Process chain under the 1894 Act: Sec 4 preliminary notification (notice that land is likely to be needed for public purpose; officers may enter and survey) -> Sec 5A hearing of objections (to the Collector within 30 days; a substantive right - the only opportunity to object) -> Sec 6 declaration (conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose; to be made within three years of Sec 4 notification until 1984 and ONE YEAR after the 1984 Amendment) -> Sec 7-8 directions to the Collector to take order for acquisition; land marked out and measured -> Sec 9 public notice to persons interested to appear and state their claims -> Sec 11 enquiry and award by the Collector -> Sec 11A (inserted 1984): award must be made within TWO YEARS of the Sec 6 declaration, else the proceedings lapse -> Sec 12: award is final and conclusive evidence as between the Collector and persons interested -> Sec 16: Collector takes possession and the land vests ABSOLUTELY in the Government, free from all encumbrances -> Sec 18: reference to Court (civil court) by a person interested who has not accepted the award - within six weeks from the date of the Collector's award if present or represented, or within six weeks of receipt of notice under Sec 12(2), or within six months of the Collector's award in other cases -> Sec 54: appeal to the High Court from the Civil Court's award.

Sec 17 URGENCY: (1) in cases of urgency the Collector may, on the expiration of 15 days from the publication of the Sec 9(1) notice, take possession of waste or arable land needed for public purpose; (4) the appropriate Government may direct that the provisions of Sec 5A shall not apply (dispensing with the hearing of objections) in cases of urgency. Misuse of Sec 17(4) was a major complaint: courts have held that dispensing with Sec 5A needs real urgency (Union of India v Mukesh Hans, 2004; Radhy Shyam v State of UP, 2011).

Sec 23: matters to be considered in determining compensation - (1) market value of the land at the date of publication of the Sec 4(1) notification; damage sustained due to taking standing crops, severing, injury to other property, change of residence/ place of business, reduction in profits; (1A) an additional amount of 12% per annum on the market value from the date of Sec 4(1) notification until the date of the award or taking of possession (added in 1984); (2) SOLATIUM - 30% of the market value in consideration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition. Sec 24: matters neglected - speculative potential, increase due to the project, disinclination of the owner to part, etc. Sec 28: interest on excess compensation awarded by Court (9% for the first year, 15% thereafter); Sec 34: interest payable by the Collector for delay in payment/ deposit of compensation (9% for the first year, then 15%). Sec 28A: right of re-determination for persons who did not seek reference but are similarly situated, if the Court has enhanced compensation for others (within three months of the Court's award).

Sec 48: the Government is at liberty to withdraw from the acquisition of any land of which possession has not been taken (and the owner is entitled to compensation for damage caused by the withdrawal). Part VII (Secs 38-44B): acquisition for companies - consent required; agreement under Sec 41; Sec 40 requirement of previous consent of the Government. Sec 3: definitions - 'land' includes benefits arising out of land and things attached to the earth. Sec 31: payment of compensation (tender; deposit in court if the owner refuses to receive or there's a dispute).
common_traps: Sec 11A: award within TWO YEARS from the Sec 6 declaration (1894 Act) - not 12 months (that is Sec 25 of the 2013 Act).
Sec 5A objections can be dispensed with only through Sec 17(4).
Sec 16 vests title ABSOLUTELY free from encumbrances (Sec 17(2) for urgency).

sections.title: RFCTLARR Act 2013 - Scheme and Process
sections.summary: The Act itself: objectives, applicability, consent, SIA, food security, notifications, timelines, award, payment and possession.
key_points: Objects: (i) fair compensation and transparency; (ii) rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R) of affected families; (iii) informed consultation and participation of affected persons (Gram Sabha, Panchayat, Municipal bodies); (iv) minimise displacement; (v) ensure that the interests of the owners of the land and other affected families are protected, and that development is sustainable.

Sec 2(1) APPLICABILITY: the Act applies when the appropriate Government acquires land for its own use, hold and control, including for Public Sector Undertakings and for public purpose, and includes the following purposes: (a) for strategic purposes relating to naval, military, air force, and armed forces of the Union, including central paramilitary forces or any work vital to national security or defence of India or State police, safety of the people; (b) for infrastructure projects (as listed, including roads, ports, power, railways, irrigation, water supply, sanitation, health, education, sports, etc.); (c) project for project affected families; (d) for planned development or improvement of village sites or any site in the urban areas or provision of land for residential purposes for the weaker sections; (e) for residential purpose to the poor or landless or to persons residing in areas affected by natural calamities; etc. Sec 2(2): the Act applies also when the appropriate Government acquires land for (a) public private partnership projects where the ownership of the land continues to vest with the Government (for public purpose) - requires consent of at least 70% of the affected families; (b) private companies for public purpose - consent of at least 80% of the affected families. 'Affected family' includes land owners and persons whose livelihood is dependent on the land (tenants, sharecroppers, agricultural labourers, artisans), forest dwellers, etc.

Sec 3: key definitions include 'appropriate Government', 'Collector', 'affected family', 'displaced family', 'land owner' (includes persons entitled to compensation, tenants and holders of forest rights), 'market value' and 'public purpose'. Consent is not required where the Government acquires land for its own use for the listed purposes; it is required for private-company and PPP acquisitions as above.

Chapter II (Secs 4-9): Determination of social impact and public purpose. Sec 4: SIA - whenever the appropriate Government intends to acquire land for a public purpose, it shall consult the concerned Panchayat, Municipality or Municipal Corporation at village level or ward level, and carry out a Social Impact Assessment study in consultation with them, in such manner and within such time as may be prescribed (within six months from the date of its commencement). Sec 5: public hearing of SIA; Sec 6: publication of SIA report in local languages and on the website; Sec 7: appraisal of the SIA report by an independent multi-disciplinary Expert Group; Sec 8: examination of proposals for land acquisition and SIA report by the appropriate Government (the Government must be satisfied that the public purpose is served, the proposed acquisition is the minimum required, and the benefits outweigh the social costs); Sec 9: exemption from SIA in the case of urgency (Sec 9 - in case of urgency, the appropriate Government may exempt the SIA, subject to the provisions of Sec 40).

Sec 10: SPECIAL PROVISION TO SAFEGUARD FOOD SECURITY - no irrigated multi-cropped land shall be acquired under this Act (except as a demonstrable last resort); wastelands to be identified for use (the total area of the land acquired in the State must not exceed the limit prescribed). Sec 11: preliminary notification - after the Expert Group's recommendation, a notification giving details of land to be acquired, the nature of public purpose, reasons for acquisition, summary of SIA, particulars of the Administrator for R&R, and place where the SIA report is available; Sec 12-15: Sec 15 - hearing of objections - any person interested may, within 60 days from the date of publication of preliminary notification, file objections to the Collector; the Collector hears and submits the report to the appropriate Government. Sec 16: R&R scheme - preparation by the Administrator; Sec 19: PUBLICATION OF DECLARATION (declaration that land is required for a public purpose) - the declaration must be made within TWELVE MONTHS from the date of publication of the preliminary notification under Sec 11 (otherwise the notification lapses - Sec 19(7)); the declaration is conclusive evidence that the land is needed for public purpose; Sec 20: land to be marked out; Sec 21: notice to persons interested; Sec 23: inquiry and award by the Collector (Sec 23: after hearing the persons interested, the Collector prepares the award of compensation and R&R); Sec 25: PERIOD WITHIN WHICH AN AWARD SHALL BE MADE - the Collector shall make an award within a period of TWELVE MONTHS from the date of publication of the declaration under Sec 19, and if no award is made within that period, the entire proceedings for the acquisition of the land shall lapse (Government may initiate fresh proceedings - the exception that where the Government extends the period for 'reasons recorded', which the court considers for validity).

Sec 38: payment of compensation and taking possession - the Collector shall take possession only after ensuring that full payment of compensation as well as rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements are paid or tendered to the entitled persons within a period of THREE MONTHS for the compensation and a period of SIX MONTHS for the monetary part of rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements listed in the Second Schedule, commencing from the date of the award made under Sec 30; infrastructural entitlements to be provided within 18 months from the date of the award (Sec 38(2)). Sec 40: SPECIAL POWERS IN CASE OF URGENCY - in case of urgency, whenever the appropriate Government so directs, the Collector, though no such award has been made, may on the expiration of 48 hours from the publication of the notice to the persons interested, take possession of any land needed for the purposes of defence of India or national security or for any emergencies arising out of natural calamities or any other emergency with the approval of the Government; compensation includes an ADDITIONAL 75% of the compensation as urgency charges (Sec 40(3)); Sec 40(2): no urgency can be invoked for any purpose other than defence/ national security or calamity; the urgency clause cannot be used for private companies or PPP.

Sec 41: SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR SCHEDULED CASTES AND SCHEDULED TRIBES - as far as possible, no acquisition in Scheduled Areas shall be made (acquisition only as a last resort); in the case of acquisition in Scheduled Areas, prior consent of the concerned Gram Sabha or Panchayats or autonomous District Councils must be obtained; the affected SC/ST families are to be resettled in the same Scheduled Area (one-third additional R&R benefits - extra benefits under Second Schedule); (Sec 41(3) - consent of Gram Sabha at the stage of SIA).

Sec 96: exemption from stamp duty and fees for transfers under the Act. Sec 101 RETURN OF UNUTILISED LAND: when any land acquired remains unutilised for a period of FIVE YEARS from the date of taking possession, it shall be returned to the original owner(s) or legal heirs, or to the Land Bank of the appropriate Government. Sec 105: the Act does not apply to the 13 enactments in the Fourth Schedule (e.g., National Highways Act, Railways Act, Atomic Energy Act, Metro Railways Acts), but the Central Government extended the compensation and R&R provisions to them by notification (28 August 2015). Sec 107: States may enact laws giving higher compensation or additional benefits. Sec 108: affected families may opt for a more beneficial State law or policy. Sec 114: repeal of the 1894 Act with savings.
common_traps: Consent: 80% for acquisition for private companies; 70% for PPP projects (Sec 2(2)); not required for the government's own use.

Sec 19(7): declaration within 12 months from Sec 11 notification; Sec 25: award within 12 months from Sec 19 declaration; Sec 38: payment within 3 months; monetary R&R within 6 months; infrastructural R&R 18 months.

Urgency clause (Sec 40) - only for defence/ national security/ natural calamities; additional 75% compensation.

Fourth Schedule enactments (e.g., National Highways Act, Railways Act, Atomic Energy Act, Metro Railways Act, Land Acquisition (Mines) Act) are exempt from the main Act, but compensation and R&R provisions were extended to them by the 2015 Order.

sections.title: Compensation and R&R under the 2013 Act (Chapter IV, V and VI)
sections.summary: Market value, multiplier, solatium, interest and the R&R entitlements are favourite numerical questions.
key_points: Sec 26 MARKET VALUE: the Collector shall adopt the following criteria in assessing and determining the market value of the land: (a) the market value, if any, specified in the Indian Stamp Act 1899 for the registration of sale deeds in the area where the land is situated; or (b) the average sale price for similar type of land situated in the nearest village or nearest vicinity area; or (c) the consented amount of compensation as agreed upon under Sec 2(2) in case of acquisition of lands for private companies or for public private partnership projects - WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. For (b), the average sale price is determined from the highest 50% of the sale deeds registered during the preceding three years in the nearest village. The date for determining the market value is the date of publication of the preliminary notification (Sec 11 notification). Sec 26(2): the market value is multiplied by a factor (1 for urban areas; between 1 and 2 for rural areas based on distance from urban area - First Schedule, as notified by the State).

Secs 27-29: buildings, trees, standing crops and other assets attached to land, and damages sustained, are valued and added. Sec 30: SOLATIUM - the Collector shall, in addition to the market value of the land as provided in Sec 26, in every case, award an amount calculated at the rate of 100% of the compensation amount (market value x multiplier + value of assets attached) in consideration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition. In addition, the Collector shall award interest at 12% per annum on the market value for the period commencing on the date of publication of the Sec 11 notification until the date of award or the date of taking possession, whichever is earlier. Total effect: compensation can be up to 2 x (market value x multiplier + assets) + interest, i.e. in rural areas up to four times the market value (in the original scheme: 'up to 4 times in rural areas and 2 times in urban areas').

SECOND SCHEDULE (R&R ENTITLEMENTS) - illustrative: provision of land for land in irrigation projects (where the acquired land is for irrigation, to the extent possible, each affected family to be allotted 1 acre of land in the command area); offer for developed land (20% of developed land for the land owners whose land is acquired for urban development - 'Land owners' compulsory acquisition for urban development projects - 20% of the developed land); houses (constructed house to affected families displaced, in rural areas of 150 sq.m plinth area, urban areas as per State rules); subsistence allowance (Rs 3,000 per month per family for a period of 12 months); one-time transport allowance (Rs 50,000); one-time resettlement allowance of Rs 50,000; jobs (employment to at least one member of the family, or lump sum of Rs 5 lakh, or annuity of Rs 2,000 per month per family for 20 years, indexed); special provisions for SC/ST families (additional benefits, e.g. one-time allowance of Rs 50,000 additional, free land for community, etc.). Third Schedule: infrastructural amenities (roads, drainage, schools, health centres, post offices, anganwadis, etc.). The figures are indicative; State rules differ.

R&R institutions: the Administrator for R&R, the Commissioner for R&R, the R&R Committee at project level, the National Monitoring Committee, and the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Authority (Sec 51) which decides references. Sec 64: a person interested who has not accepted the award may require the Collector to refer the matter to the Authority. Sec 74: appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the Authority's award or order. In Deputy Commissioner and Special Land Acquisition Officer v M/s SV Global Mill Ltd (SC, February 2026), the Court held that Sec 74 does not exclude Sec 5 of the Limitation Act 1963, so delay in appeals can be condoned for sufficient cause, including in cases begun under the 1894 Act where compensation is determined under the 2013 Act by virtue of Sec 24(1)(a).

Payment and deposit: compensation is to be paid to the persons entitled; where a person refuses to accept or there is a dispute as to title or apportionment, the amount is deposited with the Authority or court. Delay in payment attracts interest; verify the exact rate and section in the bare Act before answering a numerical question on it.

Tarsem Singh: Union of India v Tarsem Singh (2019) - the Court held that Sec 3J of the National Highways Act 1956 (which excluded the applicability of the Land Acquisition Act 1894 provisions relating to solatium and interest) is arbitrary and violative of Art 14 to the extent that it denies solatium and interest to the land owners whose land was acquired under the NH Act; accordingly, solatium and interest are payable in NH acquisitions. National Highways Act 1956: Sec 3A (notification), 3D (declaration; vesting), 3G (compensation determined by the competent authority; arbitration for disputes - Sec 3G(5)), Sec 3J. Metro Railways, Railways Act also in the Fourth Schedule; their compensation to be on the 2013 Act basis after the 2015 notification.

Compensation principles from case law: (i) market value is what a willing purchaser would pay to a willing seller; comparable sales (Sec 26(1)(b)); deduction for development cost for large tracts; (ii) a residential plot sale deed cannot be used to determine compensation for industrial land (Supreme Court, recent); (iii) compensation is to be calculated as on the date of the preliminary notification; (iv) acquisition of a part of a land; (v) tax: compensation for compulsory acquisition of agricultural land is exempt from income tax (Sec 96 of the 2013 Act; Sec 10(37) Income-tax Act for urban agricultural land compensation).

sections.title: Section 24 - Transitional Provisions and Lapse (Indore Development Authority)
sections.summary: The most litigated provision and the most likely 'case-law' question in the Land Acquisition segment. Know the text, the 5-judge Bench holding (IDA v Manoharlal, 2020), and the 2026 reaffirmations.
key_points: Sec 24(1): notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, in any case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act 1894, (a) where no award under Sec 11 of the said Land Acquisition Act has been made, then, all provisions of this Act relating to the determination of compensation shall apply; or (b) where an award under Sec 11 of the said Land Acquisition Act has been made, then such proceedings shall continue under the provisions of the said Land Acquisition Act, as if the said Act has not been repealed.

Sec 24(2): notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), in case of land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act 1894, where an award under the said Sec 11 has been made five years or more prior to the commencement of this Act but the physical possession of the land has not been taken or the compensation has not been paid, the said proceedings shall be deemed to have lapsed and the appropriate Government, if it so chooses, shall initiate the proceedings of such land acquisition afresh in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Proviso: where an award has been made and compensation in respect of a majority of land holdings has not been deposited in the account of the beneficiaries, then, all beneficiaries specified in the notification for acquisition under Sec 4 of the said Land Acquisition Act, shall be entitled to compensation in accordance with the provisions of this Act.

Pune Municipal Corporation v Harakchand Misirimal Solanki (2014) held that 'paid' means actual payment to the landowner and that deposit in court is not payment; Indore Development Authority v Shailendra (2018) (Arun Mishra J.) disagreed and referred the issue to a larger Bench; INDORE DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY v MANOHARLAL (2020) 8 SCC 129, five-judge Constitution Bench (Arun Mishra J.), overruled Pune Municipal Corporation. Holdings: (1) the word 'or' between 'possession' and 'compensation' in Sec 24(2) must be read as 'nor' or 'and' - a deemed lapse arises only when BOTH possession has not been taken AND compensation has not been paid, due to inaction of the authorities for five years or more prior to 1 January 2014; (2) 'paid' in Sec 24(2) does not include deposit of compensation in court; but if compensation was tendered and the owner refused or failed to accept it, there is no lapse (the obligation to pay is satisfied by tender; non-deposit in court does not lead to lapse; the landowner can't take advantage of his own refusal); (3) the five-year period excludes periods covered by an interim order/ stay of the court (the time during stay is excluded); (4) possession is taken in the manner prescribed by the law, i.e. by drawing a panchnama/ inquest report (the standard mode in the 1894 Act); once possession is taken, the land vests in the State free from encumbrances (Sec 16) and there is no divesting; (5) Sec 24(2) does not give rise to a new cause of action to question the legality of concluded proceedings of land acquisition; it applies to pending proceedings in which possession has not been taken or compensation has not been paid for five years (the 'cut-off' of 1 January 2014); (6) Sec 24(1)(a): if no award was made as on 1 January 2014, there is no lapse and compensation is determined under the 2013 Act; (7) the 2013 Act Sec 24 does not apply to concluded acquisitions.

Subsequent purchasers: Shiv Kumar v Union of India (2019) and later cases - subsequent purchasers have no locus standi to challenge the land acquisition or to claim lapse under Sec 24(2), because after notification under Sec 4 (and Sec 6) any transfer is void against the State (the land is encumbered by the acquisition). The Supreme Court reiterated this in a 2026 decision.

Recent Supreme Court (and High Court) decisions, including 2026 rulings, continue to apply IDA v Manoharlal: (a) acquisitions do not lapse if either possession has been taken or compensation has been tendered; (b) delay in taking possession because of litigation does not entitle the owner to the benefit of the lapse; (c) the Supreme Court has allowed delayed appeals by the Delhi Development Authority against High Court judgments that had declared DDA acquisitions lapsed under Sec 24(2) in the public interest; (d) a valid tender satisfies the obligation to pay; refusal to accept doesn't cause lapse. A person who claims lapse must prove inaction for five years prior to the commencement date.

Sec 24(1)(b) read with Sec 24(2) is the transitory regime: 'where an award has been made - the 1894 Act continues; where the award has been made five years or more before and neither possession nor compensation has been given - lapse'. The 'five years' is counted back from 1 January 2014 (i.e., the award on or before 1 January 2009).
