latest_developments.topic: Specific performance: continuous readiness and willingness
latest_developments.detail: Supreme Court judgments of 2026 (e.g., Mohammed Khaleel v Jayamma, 23 June 2026; V.N.A.S. Chandran v S. Venila, 31 July 2026) restate that Sec 16(c) SRA requires continuous readiness (financial capacity) and willingness (conduct), pleaded and proved from the date of agreement to decree; post-suit financial documents are insufficient and long unexplained delay can justify refusal of a decree. Other 2026 rulings hold that a buyer's delay in sending a legal notice is not fatal where nearly the whole price was paid (2026 INSC 573).
latest_developments.exam_use: Principle-based MCQ: 'Readiness refers to financial capacity; willingness refers to conduct.'

latest_developments.topic: Specific Relief (Amendment) Act 2018 and its prospectivity
latest_developments.detail: Specific performance is now enforceable as a general rule (Sec 10), substituted performance (Sec 20), infrastructure contracts (Secs 20A-20C, 41(ha)). The Supreme Court treats the 2018 amendments as prospective, so older agreements are tested under the unamended Act.

(1) Multiple cheques from one transaction can ground separate complaints (Jan 2026). (2) Complaint cannot be quashed at the pre-trial stage once Sec 138 ingredients are prima facie met (Renuka v State of Maharashtra, 7 Apr 2026). (3) Bank's failure to present a cheque within validity can be deficiency in service (Canara Bank v Kavita Chowdhary, Apr 2026). (4) Conviction set aside where the cheque showed patent tampering (17 July 2026). (5) Mere denial of debt does not rebut the Sec 139 presumption (4 Aug 2026). (6) An Asset Reconstruction Company can pursue Sec 138 as assignee of the loan (4 Nov 2026). (7) The Sanjabij Tari line of cases consolidates procedural directions and revisits compounding (verify exact directions in the judgment).
latest_developments.exam_use: Expect statement-type MCQs on presumption (Sec 139), jurisdiction (Sec 142(2)), interim compensation (Sec 143A), appeal deposit (Sec 148), and compounding (Sec 147).

latest_developments.topic: Land acquisition: Section 24(2) and limitation in appeals
latest_developments.detail: The Supreme Court continues to apply Indore Development Authority v Manoharlal (2020): lapse only where possession is not taken AND compensation is not paid for five years before 1 Jan 2014; subsequent purchasers lack locus. In February 2026 (Deputy Commissioner & SLAO v SV Global Mill Ltd) the Court held that Sec 74 of the 2013 Act does not exclude Sec 5 of the Limitation Act, allowing condonation of delay in appeals.
Kolkata Municipal Corporation v Bimal Kumar Shaw: seven sub-rights (notice, hearing, reasoned decision, public purpose, compensation, efficient process, conclusion).
References in the Contract Act (Sec 15 - IPC) and NI Act procedure (CrPC) are read with the new codes through the General Clauses Act; summary trial provisions now in BNSS (Secs 283-288).

Suraj Lamp (2012) continues to be cited: GPA/SA/WILL arrangements do not transfer title to immovable property; the registration of agreements to sell for Sec 53A protection has been mandatory since 2001.

distinctions.pair: Void agreement vs voidable contract vs void contract
distinctions.points: Void agreement: not enforceable from the start (Sec 2(g)); voidable: enforceable at option of aggrieved party (Sec 2(i)); void contract: valid when made, later ceases to be enforceable (Sec 2(j)).
Coercion: act forbidden by IPC/BNS or unlawful detention; undue influence: dominance of will in a relationship. Both make the contract voidable.
Fraud: intent to deceive; misrepresentation: innocent. Sec 19 diligence exception does not apply to fraud by positive statement.
Indian law (Sec 74): reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named, whichever label is used.
Two vs three parties; primary vs secondary liability.
Mortgage transfers an interest, only by act of parties; charge creates a security without transfer, by act of parties or operation of law.
Lease transfers an interest with exclusive possession; licence is a revocable personal permission (Easements Act Sec 52).
Sec 41 protects a good-faith transferee from an ostensible owner against the real owner; Sec 43 enforces the transfer against the transferor's after-acquired interest.
Sec 53A is a defence (shield) available to a transferee in possession; specific performance is the plaintiff's remedy (sword).
Temporary: until further order (CPC Order 39); perpetual: by decree on merits (Sec 38).
143A: trial court, interim compensation up to 20%, by drawer, refundable on acquittal; 148: appellate court, minimum 20% deposit of fine/compensation.
138 defines the offence; 139 raises a rebuttable presumption that the cheque was for a debt or liability.
